title: Tick-Level Trade Execution Matching via Native ASOF JOIN
human_context: In algorithmic trading, every buy or sell order must be evaluated against the most recent prevailing market quote. Standard relational equality joins fail because quotes and trades happen at irregular microsecond intervals.
hidden_trap: LLMs typically write quadratic triangular self-joins (WHERE q.ts <= t.ts) or window functions with LAG/LAST_VALUE, which create massive memory spikes on high-frequency streams.
duckdb_advantage: DuckDB native `ASOF JOIN` performs an O(N log M) binary search scan directly across partitioned timestamp indices without sorting intermediate cross products.
setup_sql:
CREATE TABLE quotes (
                quote_time TIMESTAMP,
                symbol VARCHAR,
                bid_price DOUBLE,
                ask_price DOUBLE
            );
            CREATE TABLE trades (
                trade_time TIMESTAMP,
                symbol VARCHAR,
                trade_id INT,
                executed_price DOUBLE,
                shares INT
            );
            INSERT INTO quotes VALUES
                ('2026-03-01 09:30:00.100', 'NVDA', 850.10, 850.25),
                ('2026-03-01 09:30:00.250', 'NVDA', 850.15, 850.30),
                ('2026-03-01 09:30:00.400', 'NVDA', 850.20, 850.35);
            INSERT INTO trades VALUES
                ('2026-03-01 09:30:00.150', 'NVDA', 101, 850.25, 100),
                ('2026-03-01 09:30:00.300', 'NVDA', 102, 850.30, 200),
                ('2026-03-01 09:30:00.450', 'NVDA', 103, 850.32, 150);
sql:
-- Match each executed trade with the latest market quote effective at that exact microsecond
            SELECT 
                t.trade_id,
                t.symbol,
                t.trade_time,
                t.executed_price,
                t.shares,
                q.quote_time AS prevailing_quote_time,
                q.bid_price,
                q.ask_price,
                -- Effective slippage calculation (difference between ask and executed price)
                ROUND(t.executed_price - q.ask_price, 4) AS slippage
            FROM trades t
            ASOF JOIN quotes q
              ON t.symbol = q.symbol
             AND t.trade_time >= q.quote_time
            ORDER BY t.trade_time;

title: Multi-Currency Point-in-Time FX Conversion via ASOF JOIN
human_context: Global payments systems record transactions in local currencies (EUR, JPY, GBP) that must be converted to USD using the prevailing exchange rate at the exact transaction millisecond.
hidden_trap: Joining to a daily FX table using DATE(ts) loses intraday volatility and causes currency conversion discrepancies of up to 1-2% during volatile market events.
duckdb_advantage: DuckDB's ASOF JOIN enables continuous real-time currency conversion with millisecond granularity.
sql:
-- Convert international payments to USD using the most recent point-in-time exchange rate
            SELECT 
                p.payment_id,
                p.payment_time,
                p.currency,
                p.amount_local,
                fx.rate_to_usd,
                ROUND(p.amount_local * fx.rate_to_usd, 2) AS amount_usd,
                fx.rate_time AS fx_snapshot_time
            FROM payments p
            ASOF JOIN fx_rates fx
              ON p.currency = fx.currency
             AND p.payment_time >= fx.rate_time
            ORDER BY p.payment_id;

title: Clickstream Sessionization with Inactivity Timeouts (Gaps & Islands)
human_context: Digital analytics platforms group raw user pageviews into 'sessions'. If a user is inactive for more than 30 minutes, the next click begins a brand-new session.
hidden_trap: Models mistakenly partition by user_id and take ROW_NUMBER(), which fails to segment sessions by time gaps, or use self-joins which scale quadratically.
duckdb_advantage: Window functions (LAG) combined with cumulative conditional sums (SUM(is_new_session) OVER) produce linear O(N) streaming session identifiers.
sql:
-- Detect session breaks (>30 min inactivity) and assign deterministic session UUIDs
            WITH event_lags AS (
                SELECT 
                    user_id,
                    event_time,
                    page_url,
                    -- Compare against preceding event timestamp for this user
                    LAG(event_time) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY event_time) AS prev_event_time
                FROM user_events
            ),
            session_flags AS (
                SELECT 
                    user_id,
                    event_time,
                    page_url,
                    -- Mark 1 if first event or gap exceeds 30 minutes, else 0
                    CASE 
                        WHEN prev_event_time IS NULL THEN 1
                        WHEN date_diff('second', prev_event_time, event_time) > 1800 THEN 1 
                        ELSE 0 
                    END AS is_new_session
                FROM event_lags
            )
            SELECT 
                user_id,
                event_time,
                page_url,
                -- Cumulative sum over flags establishes monotonically increasing session ID
                SUM(is_new_session) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY event_time) AS session_id
            FROM session_flags
            ORDER BY user_id, event_time;

title: Sliding Sessionization with Absolute Maximum Duration Cap
human_context: Real-world web sessions often need dual constraints: a 30-minute inactivity timeout AND a strict maximum 4-hour absolute session duration to prevent bots from maintaining endless sessions.
hidden_trap: A simple inactivity check keeps sessions alive indefinitely if events happen every 10 minutes. Tracking session origin requires window frames with state.
duckdb_advantage: DuckDB can evaluate nested window stages seamlessly with zero intermediate disk spill.
sql:
-- Partition sessions by inactivity (>30m) OR exceeding 4 hours from session start
            WITH ranked_events AS (
                SELECT 
                    user_id,
                    event_time,
                    action,
                    LAG(event_time) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY event_time) AS prev_time
                FROM bot_events
            ),
            step_flags AS (
                SELECT 
                    user_id,
                    event_time,
                    action,
                    CASE 
                        WHEN prev_time IS NULL THEN 1
                        WHEN date_diff('minute', prev_time, event_time) > 30 THEN 1
                        ELSE 0
                    END AS gap_split
                FROM ranked_events
            ),
            base_sessions AS (
                SELECT 
                    *,
                    SUM(gap_split) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY event_time) AS raw_session_id
                FROM step_flags
            )
            SELECT 
                user_id,
                event_time,
                action,
                raw_session_id,
                -- Measure elapsed minutes from session genesis
                date_diff('minute', 
                    FIRST_VALUE(event_time) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id, raw_session_id ORDER BY event_time),
                    event_time
                ) AS minutes_since_session_start
            FROM base_sessions
            ORDER BY user_id, event_time;

title: IoT Sensor Telemetry Gap-Filling via generate_series and LOCF
human_context: Industrial IoT sensors emit readings intermittently to save bandwidth. Downstream machine learning models require strict continuous 1-minute time grids with Last Observation Carried Forward (LOCF).
hidden_trap: Using OUTER JOIN without dynamic range generation leaves temporal voids, leading to missing periods in downstream feature stores.
duckdb_advantage: DuckDB `generate_series` produces virtual timestamp arrays directly joined with windowed `IGNORE NULLS` forward-fills.
sql:
-- Resample sparse telemetry into continuous 1-minute intervals with Last Observation Carried Forward
            WITH time_grid AS (
                SELECT UNNEST(generate_series(
                    TIMESTAMP '2026-03-01 08:00:00',
                    TIMESTAMP '2026-03-01 08:05:00',
                    INTERVAL '1 minute'
                )) AS bucket_time
            ),
            aligned_readings AS (
                SELECT 
                    grid.bucket_time,
                    42 AS device_id,
                    st.temperature
                FROM time_grid grid
                LEFT JOIN sensor_telemetry st
                  ON grid.bucket_time = st.recorded_at
                 AND st.device_id = 42
            )
            SELECT 
                bucket_time,
                device_id,
                temperature AS raw_reading,
                -- Forward fill the most recent non-null temperature
                COALESCE(
                    temperature,
                    LAST_VALUE(temperature IGNORE NULLS) OVER (
                        PARTITION BY device_id 
                        ORDER BY bucket_time 
                        ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
                    )
                ) AS filled_temperature
            FROM aligned_readings
            ORDER BY bucket_time;

title: Bitemporal Auditing: Valid-Time vs. Transaction-Time Alignment
human_context: Financial compliance requires knowing: 'What did we believe customer Alice's credit limit was on May 15th, based on what was entered into our database as of June 1st?' (Bitemporal query).
hidden_trap: Relying on a single timestamp column confuses retroactive corrections with real-world effective dates, causing compliance audit failures.
duckdb_advantage: DuckDB can evaluate dual closed-open temporal intervals (`[valid_from, valid_to)` and `[system_from, system_to)`) with high-speed range predicates.
setup_sql:
CREATE TABLE credit_limits_audit (
                customer_id INT,
                credit_limit DECIMAL(10,2),
                valid_from DATE,
                valid_to DATE,
                system_from TIMESTAMP,
                system_to TIMESTAMP
            );
            INSERT INTO credit_limits_audit VALUES
                -- Original belief entered on May 1st
                (501, 5000.00, '2026-05-01', '2026-12-31', '2026-05-01 09:00:00', '2026-06-01 10:00:00'),
                -- Retroactive correction entered on June 1st backdating Alice's limit to $8,000 effective May 15th
                (501, 8000.00, '2026-05-15', '2026-12-31', '2026-06-01 10:00:00', '9999-12-31 23:59:59');
sql:
-- Query credit limit effective on 2026-05-20 as known to the system on 2026-05-25 (before retroactive update)
            SELECT 
                customer_id,
                credit_limit AS limit_as_known_then,
                valid_from,
                valid_to,
                system_from,
                system_to
            FROM credit_limits_audit
            WHERE customer_id = 501
              -- As-of Business Date: 2026-05-20
              AND DATE '2026-05-20' >= valid_from 
              AND DATE '2026-05-20' < valid_to
              -- As-of System State: 2026-05-25
              AND TIMESTAMP '2026-05-25 00:00:00' >= system_from 
              AND TIMESTAMP '2026-05-25 00:00:00' < system_to;

title: Slowly Changing Dimension Type 2 Join with Open-Ended Future
human_context: Customers change addresses or account tiers over time. Joining historical orders to customer profile dimensions requires matching the order date to the active validity interval.
hidden_trap: Current active records typically have `valid_to IS NULL`. A simple `order_date BETWEEN valid_from AND valid_to` drops all current active records.
duckdb_advantage: DuckDB optimizes COALESCE null bounds directly into range filter pushdown.
sql:
-- Join fact orders to historical customer dimension without dropping active records
            SELECT 
                o.order_id,
                o.customer_id,
                o.order_date,
                o.amount,
                c.tier AS customer_tier_at_purchase
            FROM fact_orders o
            JOIN dim_customer_scd c
              ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
             AND o.order_date >= c.valid_from
             AND o.order_date < COALESCE(c.valid_to, DATE '9999-12-31')
            ORDER BY o.order_id;

title: Hopping / Overlapping Window Aggregations via time_bucket
human_context: Real-time surveillance monitors rolling 15-minute average latency stepped forward every 5 minutes (a hopping window).
hidden_trap: Standard GROUP BY time_bucket only produces non-overlapping tumbling windows, missing cross-boundary bursts.
duckdb_advantage: DuckDB can evaluate multi-frequency time_bucket queries combined with generate_series hops in memory.
sql:
-- Generate 15-minute sliding windows stepped every 5 minutes (hopping window)
            WITH window_steps AS (
                SELECT UNNEST(generate_series(
                    TIMESTAMP '2026-03-01 10:00:00',
                    TIMESTAMP '2026-03-01 10:15:00',
                    INTERVAL '5 minutes'
                )) AS window_start
            )
            SELECT 
                w.window_start,
                w.window_start + INTERVAL '15 minutes' AS window_end,
                m.server_id,
                COUNT(m.cpu_utilization) AS sample_count,
                ROUND(AVG(m.cpu_utilization), 2) AS avg_cpu,
                MAX(m.cpu_utilization) AS peak_cpu
            FROM window_steps w
            JOIN server_metrics m
              ON m.metric_time >= w.window_start
             AND m.metric_time < w.window_start + INTERVAL '15 minutes'
            GROUP BY w.window_start, m.server_id
            ORDER BY w.window_start;

title: Financial Ledger Cumulative Balance with Duplicate Timestamp Ties
human_context: Ledger entries can occur at the exact same millisecond. Financial ledgers must preserve strict incremental balances rather than bunching peer rows.
hidden_trap: SQL window functions default to `RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW`, which aggregates identical timestamps together into the same running total.
duckdb_advantage: Explicit `ROWS BETWEEN` frames guarantee deterministic transaction-by-transaction cumulative balances.
sql:
-- Calculate strict running ledger balance using ROWS frame to prevent peer bunching
            SELECT 
                entry_id,
                account_id,
                posted_time,
                amount,
                -- ROWS frame evaluates row-by-row even when posted_time is identical
                SUM(amount) OVER (
                    PARTITION BY account_id
                    ORDER BY posted_time, entry_id
                    ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
                ) AS running_balance
            FROM ledger
            ORDER BY posted_time, entry_id;

title: Window Frame Exclusion: Peer Period Average via EXCLUDE CURRENT ROW
human_context: To detect anomalous spikes, analysts compare a metric against the average of neighboring days, strictly excluding the current day's value to avoid skewing the baseline.
hidden_trap: Computing rolling averages without excluding the current row inflates the baseline during the spike itself, hiding the anomaly.
duckdb_advantage: DuckDB supports standard SQL:2011 window frame exclusion clauses: `EXCLUDE CURRENT ROW`.
setup_sql:
CREATE TABLE daily_api_calls (
                service_id VARCHAR,
                call_date DATE,
                total_calls INT
            );
            INSERT INTO daily_api_calls VALUES
                ('auth-svc', '2026-03-01', 1000),
                ('auth-svc', '2026-03-02', 1050),
                ('auth-svc', '2026-03-03', 9500), -- Major spike
                ('auth-svc', '2026-03-04', 1020),
                ('auth-svc', '2026-03-05', 1010);
sql:
-- Calculate 5-day baseline average strictly excluding current row
            SELECT 
                service_id,
                call_date,
                total_calls,
                -- 2 days before and 2 days after, excluding current day
                ROUND(AVG(total_calls) OVER (
                    PARTITION BY service_id
                    ORDER BY call_date
                    ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND 2 FOLLOWING
                    EXCLUDE CURRENT ROW
                ), 2) AS peer_baseline_avg,
                -- Spikiness ratio
                ROUND(total_calls / AVG(total_calls) OVER (
                    PARTITION BY service_id
                    ORDER BY call_date
                    ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND 2 FOLLOWING
                    EXCLUDE CURRENT ROW
                ), 2) AS spike_factor
            FROM daily_api_calls
            ORDER BY call_date;

title: Excluding Ties in Percentile Ranks via EXCLUDE TIES
human_context: When evaluating employee sales performance, ties should not inflate the percentile score against colleagues who achieved the exact same result.
hidden_trap: Using standard RANK() causes tied individuals to push each other's percentiles higher or lower inconsistently.
duckdb_advantage: DuckDB's `EXCLUDE TIES` window frame syntax accurately handles identical duplicate metrics.
sql:
-- Compute cumulative sales sum excluding tied peers in current row calculation
            SELECT 
                rep_id,
                sales_quota_achieved,
                SUM(sales_quota_achieved) OVER (
                    ORDER BY sales_quota_achieved DESC
                    RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
                    EXCLUDE TIES
                ) AS cumulative_sales_exclusive_of_ties
            FROM rep_sales
            ORDER BY sales_quota_achieved DESC, rep_id;

title: Inter-Packet Network Arrival Jitter at Nanosecond Resolution
human_context: High-speed network telemetry measures packet arrival jitter (variance in inter-packet delay). Jitter spikes indicate network congestion or buffer bloat.
hidden_trap: Standard SQL datetime arithmetic truncates to milliseconds or seconds, losing high-frequency microsecond microbursts.
duckdb_advantage: DuckDB natively supports `epoch_ns` and TIMESTAMP with microsecond/nanosecond fidelity.
sql:
-- Compute inter-packet arrival delta in microseconds and identify variance
            WITH deltas AS (
                SELECT 
                    packet_id,
                    captured_at,
                    date_diff('microsecond', 
                        LAG(captured_at) OVER (ORDER BY captured_at), 
                        captured_at
                    ) AS delta_microseconds
                FROM packet_stream
            )
            SELECT 
                packet_id,
                captured_at,
                delta_microseconds,
                -- Measure moving jitter variance over last 3 packets
                ROUND(STDDEV(delta_microseconds) OVER (
                    ORDER BY captured_at 
                    ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
                ), 2) AS rolling_jitter_stddev
            FROM deltas
            ORDER BY captured_at;

title: Point-in-Time Limit Order Book (LOB) State Reconstruction
human_context: Market microstructure researchers need to reconstruct the exact bids and asks available at an arbitrary point in time from an append-only event stream of place, cancel, and fill orders.
hidden_trap: Summing active orders without filtering out cancellations that occurred before the target time produces a phantom order book.
duckdb_advantage: DuckDB can evaluate event lifespans and aggregate active depth efficiently in a single scan.
setup_sql:
CREATE TABLE order_events (
                event_id INT,
                order_id INT,
                event_type VARCHAR, -- 'INSERT', 'CANCEL', 'FILL'
                side VARCHAR,       -- 'BID', 'ASK'
                price DOUBLE,
                quantity INT,
                event_time TIMESTAMP
            );
            INSERT INTO order_events VALUES
                (1, 101, 'INSERT', 'BID', 100.50, 10, '2026-03-01 09:30:01'),
                (2, 102, 'INSERT', 'BID', 100.25, 20, '2026-03-01 09:30:02'),
                (3, 101, 'CANCEL', 'BID', 100.50, 10, '2026-03-01 09:30:05'),
                (4, 103, 'INSERT', 'BID', 100.60, 15, '2026-03-01 09:30:06');
sql:
-- Reconstruct order book state at exactly 09:30:05
            WITH snapshot_events AS (
                SELECT *
                FROM order_events
                WHERE event_time <= TIMESTAMP '2026-03-01 09:30:05'
            ),
            active_orders AS (
                SELECT 
                    order_id,
                    side,
                    price,
                    -- Net quantity remaining after cancellations/fills
                    SUM(CASE WHEN event_type = 'INSERT' THEN quantity ELSE -quantity END) AS remaining_qty
                FROM snapshot_events
                GROUP BY order_id, side, price
                HAVING SUM(CASE WHEN event_type = 'INSERT' THEN quantity ELSE -quantity END) > 0
            )
            SELECT 
                side,
                price,
                SUM(remaining_qty) AS aggregate_depth
            FROM active_orders
            GROUP BY side, price
            ORDER BY price DESC;

title: Time-Weighted Average Price (TWAP) with Variable Interval Weights
human_context: TWAP measures the average price of an asset weighted by the duration of time that each price level was sustained, preventing brief price spikes from distorting valuation.
hidden_trap: Taking simple AVG(price) biases the result towards periods with frequent tick updates rather than sustained duration.
duckdb_advantage: DuckDB LEAD functions cleanly calculate elapsed durations between price revisions.
setup_sql:
CREATE TABLE price_ticks (
                tick_time TIMESTAMP,
                symbol VARCHAR,
                price DOUBLE
            );
            INSERT INTO price_ticks VALUES
                ('2026-03-01 10:00:00', 'ETH', 3000.00), -- lasted 10 min
                ('2026-03-01 10:10:00', 'ETH', 3050.00), -- lasted 20 min
                ('2026-03-01 10:30:00', 'ETH', 3010.00), -- lasted 30 min
                ('2026-03-01 11:00:00', 'ETH', 3010.00); -- window end
sql:
-- Calculate 1-hour TWAP from 10:00 to 11:00
            WITH tick_durations AS (
                SELECT 
                    symbol,
                    tick_time,
                    price,
                    date_diff('second', tick_time, 
                        LEAD(tick_time, 1, TIMESTAMP '2026-03-01 11:00:00') OVER (PARTITION BY symbol ORDER BY tick_time)
                    ) AS duration_seconds
                FROM price_ticks
                WHERE tick_time < TIMESTAMP '2026-03-01 11:00:00'
            )
            SELECT 
                symbol,
                ROUND(SUM(price * duration_seconds) / SUM(duration_seconds), 2) AS twap_price,
                SUM(duration_seconds) AS total_duration_seconds
            FROM tick_durations
            GROUP BY symbol;

title: Intraday Volume-Weighted Average Price (VWAP) Resetting Daily
human_context: VWAP provides institutional traders the definitive benchmark price weighted by traded volume, resetting to zero at the start of every trading day.
hidden_trap: Failing to partition by trading date mixes multi-day volume into the intraday numerator and denominator.
duckdb_advantage: DuckDB calculates cumulative sums in a single pass without subqueries.
setup_sql:
CREATE TABLE market_trades (
                symbol VARCHAR,
                trade_time TIMESTAMP,
                price DOUBLE,
                volume INT
            );
            INSERT INTO market_trades VALUES
                ('AAPL', '2026-03-01 09:35:00', 180.00, 1000),
                ('AAPL', '2026-03-01 09:40:00', 181.00, 2000),
                ('AAPL', '2026-03-02 09:35:00', 182.00, 500); -- Next day reset
sql:
-- Intraday continuous VWAP calculation
            SELECT 
                symbol,
                trade_time,
                price,
                volume,
                ROUND(
                    SUM(price * volume) OVER (
                        PARTITION BY symbol, CAST(trade_time AS DATE)
                        ORDER BY trade_time
                        ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
                    ) / 
                    SUM(volume) OVER (
                        PARTITION BY symbol, CAST(trade_time AS DATE)
                        ORDER BY trade_time
                        ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
                    ), 2
                ) AS intraday_vwap
            FROM market_trades
            ORDER BY symbol, trade_time;

title: Chronological Multi-Stage Conversion Funnel with Time Boundaries
human_context: In product funnels (Signup -> Verify -> Purchase), events must occur in exact chronological order, with each step completed within 24 hours of the previous.
hidden_trap: Models join events without checking timestamp ordering (e.g., verifying after purchase), artificially inflating funnel conversion.
duckdb_advantage: DuckDB QUALIFY and chained CTEs preserve strict chronological order with pushdown predicates.
setup_sql:
CREATE TABLE user_actions (
                user_id INT,
                stage VARCHAR,
                action_time TIMESTAMP
            );
            INSERT INTO user_actions VALUES
                (1, 'signup',   '2026-03-01 10:00:00'),
                (1, 'verify',   '2026-03-01 11:00:00'),
                (1, 'purchase', '2026-03-01 15:00:00'),
                (2, 'signup',   '2026-03-01 10:00:00'),
                (2, 'purchase', '2026-03-01 10:30:00'); -- Skipped verify
sql:
-- Enforce Signup -> Verify -> Purchase chronological order
            WITH step1 AS (
                SELECT user_id, action_time AS signup_time
                FROM user_actions
                WHERE stage = 'signup'
            ),
            step2 AS (
                SELECT s1.user_id, s1.signup_time, MIN(a.action_time) AS verify_time
                FROM step1 s1
                JOIN user_actions a 
                  ON s1.user_id = a.user_id 
                 AND a.stage = 'verify'
                 AND a.action_time >= s1.signup_time
                 AND a.action_time <= s1.signup_time + INTERVAL '24 hours'
                GROUP BY s1.user_id, s1.signup_time
            ),
            step3 AS (
                SELECT s2.user_id, s2.signup_time, s2.verify_time, MIN(a.action_time) AS purchase_time
                FROM step2 s2
                JOIN user_actions a 
                  ON s2.user_id = a.user_id 
                 AND a.stage = 'purchase'
                 AND a.action_time >= s2.verify_time
                 AND a.action_time <= s2.verify_time + INTERVAL '24 hours'
                GROUP BY s2.user_id, s2.signup_time, s2.verify_time
            )
            SELECT 
                COUNT(s1.user_id) AS total_signups,
                COUNT(s2.user_id) AS verified_users,
                COUNT(s3.user_id) AS completed_purchasers,
                ROUND(COUNT(s3.user_id) * 100.0 / COUNT(s1.user_id), 1) AS end_to_end_conversion_pct
            FROM step1 s1
            LEFT JOIN step2 s2 ON s1.user_id = s2.user_id
            LEFT JOIN step3 s3 ON s1.user_id = s3.user_id;

title: Dynamic User Retention Cohort Matrix by Weekly Milestones
human_context: SaaS analytics track weekly retention curves (Day 0, Day 7, Day 14, Day 30) based on user signup week.
hidden_trap: Calculating retention without dynamic date grouping produces rigid, fragile queries requiring manual updates every week.
duckdb_advantage: DuckDB date_trunc and conditional aggregation build clean dynamic cohort tables.
sql:
-- Generate dynamic cohort retention matrix
            SELECT 
                date_trunc('week', u.signup_date) AS cohort_week,
                COUNT(DISTINCT u.user_id) AS cohort_size,
                COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN a.activity_date = u.signup_date THEN u.user_id END) AS day_0_active,
                COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN a.activity_date >= u.signup_date + 7 AND a.activity_date < u.signup_date + 14 THEN u.user_id END) AS day_7_active,
                COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN a.activity_date >= u.signup_date + 14 AND a.activity_date < u.signup_date + 21 THEN u.user_id END) AS day_14_active
            FROM app_users u
            LEFT JOIN activity_log a ON u.user_id = a.user_id
            GROUP BY cohort_week
            ORDER BY cohort_week;

title: Exponential Time-Decayed User Affinity Scoring
human_context: Recommendation systems score user interest where recent clicks count significantly more than clicks from 30 days ago, modeled via exponential decay: score * e^(-lambda * delta_days).
hidden_trap: Equal-weight counts overemphasize obsolete user interests from months ago.
duckdb_advantage: DuckDB vector math supports mathematical functions (`EXP`, `POW`) directly in aggregation pipelines.
setup_sql:
CREATE TABLE item_clicks (
                user_id INT,
                category VARCHAR,
                click_time TIMESTAMP
            );
            INSERT INTO item_clicks VALUES
                (99, 'laptops', '2026-03-01 10:00:00'), -- Today
                (99, 'laptops', '2026-02-20 10:00:00'), -- 9 days ago
                (99, 'shoes',   '2026-01-01 10:00:00'); -- 60 days ago
sql:
-- Exponential decay affinity score with 7-day half-life (lambda = ln(2)/7 = ~0.099)
            SELECT 
                user_id,
                category,
                ROUND(SUM(
                    EXP(-0.099 * date_diff('day', click_time, TIMESTAMP '2026-03-01 12:00:00'))
                ), 3) AS decayed_affinity_score
            FROM item_clicks
            GROUP BY user_id, category
            ORDER BY decayed_affinity_score DESC;

title: Customer Churn Anomaly Detection vs Historical Purchase Rhythm
human_context: A customer who normally buys every 3 days is at risk if they haven't bought in 10 days. But a customer who buys quarterly is not. Churn detection must be personalized to each user's cadence.
hidden_trap: Static 30-day churn thresholds misflag seasonal or low-frequency high-value customers.
duckdb_advantage: DuckDB window functions compute user-specific median purchase intervals.
setup_sql:
CREATE TABLE orders_history (
                customer_id INT,
                order_date DATE
            );
            INSERT INTO orders_history VALUES
                (1, '2026-01-01'), (1, '2026-01-04'), (1, '2026-01-07'), -- Rhythm: 3 days
                (2, '2026-01-01'), (2, '2026-02-01'), (2, '2026-03-01'); -- Rhythm: 30 days
sql:
-- Calculate median inter-purchase days and compare against days elapsed since latest order
            WITH purchase_intervals AS (
                SELECT 
                    customer_id,
                    order_date,
                    order_date - LAG(order_date) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY order_date) AS days_between
                FROM orders_history
            ),
            user_cadence AS (
                SELECT 
                    customer_id,
                    MAX(order_date) AS last_order_date,
                    MEDIAN(days_between) AS median_purchase_interval_days
                FROM purchase_intervals
                GROUP BY customer_id
            )
            SELECT 
                customer_id,
                last_order_date,
                median_purchase_interval_days,
                (DATE '2026-03-10' - last_order_date) AS days_since_last_order,
                CASE 
                    WHEN (DATE '2026-03-10' - last_order_date) > (2.5 * median_purchase_interval_days) 
                    THEN 'HIGH_CHURN_RISK' 
                    ELSE 'NORMAL' 
                END AS churn_risk_status
            FROM user_cadence
            ORDER BY customer_id;

title: Peak Concurrent Workforce Capacity via Interval Overlap Scan
human_context: Workforce managers must calculate maximum concurrent staffing levels from employee shift start and end times to ensure warehouse safety limits are never breached.
hidden_trap: Pairwise self-joins between overlapping shifts blow up to O(N^2) complexity.
duckdb_advantage: Transforming shifts into discrete (+1 start, -1 end) point events reduces peak concurrency calculation to a single O(N log N) streaming pass.
sql:
-- Transform start/end intervals into delta events and compute peak concurrent staffing
            WITH shift_events AS (
                SELECT start_time AS event_time, 1 AS delta FROM staff_shifts
                UNION ALL
                SELECT end_time AS event_time, -1 AS delta FROM staff_shifts
            ),
            running_occupancy AS (
                SELECT 
                    event_time,
                    SUM(delta) OVER (ORDER BY event_time, delta DESC) AS concurrent_workers
                FROM shift_events
            )
            SELECT 
                MAX(concurrent_workers) AS peak_concurrent_workers
            FROM running_occupancy;

title: Continuous Asset Lease Unallocated Gap Discovery
human_context: Fleet managers track commercial vehicles to find idle 'unrented' gaps between back-to-back rental contracts for fleet utilization auditing.
hidden_trap: Comparing each row with LEAD without filtering where next_start > current_end misses adjacent non-overlapping bookings.
duckdb_advantage: DuckDB window functions compute discrete idle intervals in a single scan.
setup_sql:
CREATE TABLE vehicle_leases (
                vehicle_id INT,
                lease_start DATE,
                lease_end DATE
            );
            INSERT INTO vehicle_leases VALUES
                (55, '2026-01-01', '2026-01-10'),
                (55, '2026-01-15', '2026-01-20'), -- 5 day gap (Jan 10 - Jan 15)
                (55, '2026-01-20', '2026-01-30'); -- contiguous
sql:
-- Identify idle intervals between vehicle leases
            WITH lease_boundaries AS (
                SELECT 
                    vehicle_id,
                    lease_end AS gap_start,
                    LEAD(lease_start) OVER (PARTITION BY vehicle_id ORDER BY lease_start) AS gap_end
                FROM vehicle_leases
            )
            SELECT 
                vehicle_id,
                gap_start,
                gap_end,
                (gap_end - gap_start) AS idle_days
            FROM lease_boundaries
            WHERE gap_end IS NOT NULL 
              AND gap_end > gap_start
            ORDER BY vehicle_id, gap_start;

title: Bi-directional Linear Value Interpolation between Observations
human_context: When a sensor drops offline for 30 minutes, data scientists prefer linear interpolation between the last known reading and the next recovered reading rather than flat zero-filling.
hidden_trap: Requires simultaneous look-behind (LAG) and look-ahead (LEAD) across varying time distances.
duckdb_advantage: DuckDB calculates multi-point interpolation in a single query.
sql:
-- Linearly interpolate missing PSI values based on preceding and following known points
            WITH bounds AS (
                SELECT 
                    ts,
                    psi,
                    LAST_VALUE(psi IGNORE NULLS) OVER (ORDER BY ts ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS prev_psi,
                    LAST_VALUE(ts IGNORE NULLS) OVER (ORDER BY ts ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS prev_ts,
                    FIRST_VALUE(psi IGNORE NULLS) OVER (ORDER BY ts ROWS BETWEEN CURRENT ROW AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING) AS next_psi,
                    FIRST_VALUE(ts IGNORE NULLS) OVER (ORDER BY ts ROWS BETWEEN CURRENT ROW AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING) AS next_ts
                FROM pressure_readings
            )
            SELECT 
                ts,
                psi AS raw_psi,
                CASE 
                    WHEN psi IS NOT NULL THEN psi
                    ELSE ROUND(
                        prev_psi + (next_psi - prev_psi) * 
                        (date_diff('second', prev_ts, ts) * 1.0 / date_diff('second', prev_ts, next_ts)), 2
                    )
                END AS interpolated_psi
            FROM bounds
            ORDER BY ts;

title: Outlier-Resistant Rolling Window (Trimmed Mean Aggregation)
human_context: Financial risk models compute a 7-day rolling average excluding the highest and lowest single observations in each 7-day window to eliminate transient flash crashes.
hidden_trap: Writing self-joins with sub-aggregations to filter min/max results in huge query execution trees.
duckdb_advantage: DuckDB window functions compute rolling sum, min, and max in parallel O(1) passes.
sql:
-- Calculate trimmed rolling mean excluding min and max values within a 5-day window
            WITH windowed_stats AS (
                SELECT 
                    trade_date,
                    settlement_amount,
                    COUNT(*) OVER w AS win_count,
                    SUM(settlement_amount) OVER w AS win_sum,
                    MIN(settlement_amount) OVER w AS win_min,
                    MAX(settlement_amount) OVER w AS win_max
                FROM daily_settlement
                WINDOW w AS (ORDER BY trade_date ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND 2 FOLLOWING)
            )
            SELECT 
                trade_date,
                settlement_amount,
                -- Subtract min and max from sum and divide by (count - 2)
                CASE 
                    WHEN win_count > 2 THEN ROUND((win_sum - win_min - win_max) / (win_count - 2), 2)
                    ELSE settlement_amount
                END AS trimmed_mean_5d
            FROM windowed_stats
            ORDER BY trade_date;

title: SARGable Fiscal Year Date Range Partition Pruning
human_context: Data warehouses partition petabyte event tables by date. Wrapping date columns in functions (e.g. `WHERE strftime('%Y', event_time) = '2026'`) breaks partition pruning, forcing a full table scan.
hidden_trap: Non-SARGable functions force DuckDB/Snowflake to scan every Parquet row group.
duckdb_advantage: Direct boundary comparison (`>= '2026-01-01' AND < '2027-01-01'`) allows DuckDB to prune Parquet files via metadata statistics.
sql:
-- Exact SARGable half-open date boundary pruning
            SELECT 
                event_id,
                event_timestamp,
                payload
            FROM telemetry_partitions
            WHERE event_timestamp >= TIMESTAMP '2026-01-01 00:00:00'
              AND event_timestamp <  TIMESTAMP '2027-01-01 00:00:00'
            ORDER BY event_timestamp;

title: Multi-Touch Marketing Attribution Comparison in a Single Pass
human_context: CMOs need to compare 3 attribution models (First-Touch, Last-Touch, and Uniform Linear) for touchpoints occurring within 30 days prior to conversion.
hidden_trap: Running three separate join queries triples warehouse compute costs and risks data inconsistency.
duckdb_advantage: DuckDB window functions compute First-Touch, Last-Touch, and touchpoint counts simultaneously in one query.
sql:
-- Multi-touch attribution comparison (First-touch, Last-touch, Linear)
            WITH eligible_touches AS (
                SELECT 
                    c.user_id,
                    c.revenue,
                    a.channel,
                    a.click_time,
                    ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY c.user_id ORDER BY a.click_time ASC) AS touch_asc,
                    ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY c.user_id ORDER BY a.click_time DESC) AS touch_desc,
                    COUNT(*) OVER (PARTITION BY c.user_id) AS total_touches
                FROM conversions c
                JOIN ad_clicks a 
                  ON c.user_id = a.user_id 
                 AND a.click_time >= c.conversion_time - INTERVAL '30 days'
                 AND a.click_time <= c.conversion_time
            )
            SELECT 
                channel,
                -- First Touch: 100% credit if first
                SUM(CASE WHEN touch_asc = 1 THEN revenue ELSE 0 END) AS first_touch_revenue,
                -- Last Touch: 100% credit if last
                SUM(CASE WHEN touch_desc = 1 THEN revenue ELSE 0 END) AS last_touch_revenue,
                -- Linear: Equal credit across all touchpoints
                ROUND(SUM(revenue / total_touches), 2) AS linear_touch_revenue
            FROM eligible_touches
            GROUP BY channel
            ORDER BY channel;

title: Dense Vector Cosine Similarity Nearest Neighbors (Top-K ANN)
human_context: When a user asks a question in an AI assistant, the query is embedded into a dense vector (e.g. 4-dimensional here for illustration, or 384/1536 in prod). We retrieve the top most semantically relevant documentation chunks.
hidden_trap: Models frequently try to calculate cosine similarity manually using dot product divided by norms in SQL, which is slow, verbose, and numerically unstable with zero vectors.
duckdb_advantage: DuckDB has high-performance native SIMD-accelerated `array_cosine_similarity(a, b)` over fixed-size arrays `FLOAT[N]`.
sql:
-- Find the top 2 documents closest to the query embedding [0.9, 0.1, 0.25, 0.0]
            WITH scored_docs AS (
                SELECT 
                    doc_id,
                    title,
                    embedding,
                    -- Native SIMD cosine similarity
                    array_cosine_similarity(embedding, [0.9, 0.1, 0.25, 0.0]::FLOAT[4]) AS cosine_score
                FROM doc_embeddings
            )
            SELECT 
                doc_id,
                title,
                ROUND(cosine_score, 4) AS similarity_score
            FROM scored_docs
            ORDER BY cosine_score DESC
            LIMIT 2;

title: L2 Euclidean Distance Nearest Neighbors Search via array_distance
human_context: In computer vision feature retrieval (facial recognition, product image matching), feature vectors are compared using Euclidean (L2) distance where lower distance equals higher visual similarity.
hidden_trap: LLMs often try to write SQRT(SUM(POW(a - b, 2))) which prevents vectorized hardware acceleration.
duckdb_advantage: DuckDB provides native `array_distance(a, b)` for Euclidean L2 metric calculation.
sql:
-- Find visual nearest neighbors to query image vector [1.05, 2.05, 3.0]
            SELECT 
                image_id,
                label,
                ROUND(array_distance(vector, [1.05, 2.05, 3.0]::FLOAT[3]), 4) AS l2_distance
            FROM image_features
            ORDER BY l2_distance ASC
            LIMIT 2;

title: Maximum Inner Product Search (MIPS) for Normalized Embeddings
human_context: For unit-normalized vectors (e.g. OpenAI text-embedding-3 or Cohere embeddings), cosine similarity is identical to the inner product (dot product), which executes even faster.
hidden_trap: Re-normalizing vectors in every query wastes compute when embeddings are pre-normalized upon insertion.
duckdb_advantage: DuckDB native `array_inner_product(a, b)` provides the fastest dot-product vector scoring path.
sql:
-- MIPS search for normalized user query vector [0.85, 0.52, 0.0]
            SELECT 
                product_id,
                product_name,
                ROUND(array_inner_product(norm_vector, [0.85, 0.52, 0.0]::FLOAT[3]), 4) AS dot_product_score
            FROM product_catalog_vectors
            ORDER BY dot_product_score DESC
            LIMIT 2;

title: The Pre-Filtering Trap: Relational Predicates with Vector Top-K
human_context: A user searches for 'cheap mechanical keyboard under $50'. If you run vector search Top-K first and filter by price afterwards (post-filtering), you may return zero products because all top-5 matches were $150 keyboards.
hidden_trap: Post-filtering vector results breaks recall. Relational constraints (in-stock, price bounds, user tenant_id) must be evaluated as PRE-FILTERS before Top-K ranking.
duckdb_advantage: DuckDB seamlessly pushes relational filters directly into the scan before computing expensive vector distances.
setup_sql:
CREATE TABLE inventory_items (
                item_id INT,
                name VARCHAR,
                price DECIMAL(10,2),
                in_stock BOOLEAN,
                vector FLOAT[3]
            );
            INSERT INTO inventory_items VALUES
                (1, 'Custom Mechanical Keyboard', 180.00, true,  [0.9, 0.1, 0.1]::FLOAT[3]),
                (2, 'Budget Gaming Keyboard',       45.00, true,  [0.85, 0.15, 0.1]::FLOAT[3]),
                (3, 'Cheap Office Keyboard',        25.00, true,  [0.8, 0.2, 0.1]::FLOAT[3]),
                (4, 'Out of Stock Keyboard',        35.00, false, [0.92, 0.1, 0.1]::FLOAT[3]);
sql:
-- Pre-filtered vector search: strictly in-stock and under $50 BEFORE ranking top 2
            SELECT 
                item_id,
                name,
                price,
                ROUND(array_cosine_similarity(vector, [0.9, 0.1, 0.1]::FLOAT[3]), 4) AS similarity
            FROM inventory_items
            WHERE in_stock = true
              AND price <= 50.00
            ORDER BY similarity DESC
            LIMIT 2;

title: Adaptive Similarity Thresholding with Fallback Top-K Guarantee
human_context: RAG systems want high-confidence matches (similarity > 0.85) to avoid hallucinations, but if no document exceeds 0.85, they need a guaranteed top-1 fallback to provide at least some context.
hidden_trap: A hard WHERE similarity > 0.85 yields empty sets, while a raw LIMIT 5 includes irrelevant noise.
duckdb_advantage: DuckDB window functions and conditional filtering allow hybrid thresholding in a single query.
sql:
-- Score items, guarantee top 1 fallback even if below 0.85 threshold
            WITH scored AS (
                SELECT 
                    kb_id,
                    content,
                    array_cosine_similarity(vector, [0.9, 0.2, 0.1]::FLOAT[3]) AS sim_score,
                    ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY array_cosine_similarity(vector, [0.9, 0.2, 0.1]::FLOAT[3]) DESC) AS rank_pos
                FROM knowledge_base
            )
            SELECT 
                kb_id,
                content,
                ROUND(sim_score, 4) AS sim_score,
                rank_pos,
                CASE WHEN sim_score >= 0.85 THEN 'CONFIDENT_MATCH' ELSE 'FALLBACK_TOP_MATCH' END AS match_type
            FROM scored
            WHERE sim_score >= 0.85 OR rank_pos = 1
            ORDER BY rank_pos;

title: Semantic Deduplication of IT Incident Tickets via Vector Cosine Threshold
human_context: During service outages, hundreds of users submit identically phrased IT support tickets ('login down', 'cannot access account'). Clustering tickets with vector similarity > 0.88 consolidates duplicates into a single incident.
hidden_trap: Quadratic N x N self-joins without ordering check (`t1.id < t2.id`) double compute and compare tickets to themselves.
duckdb_advantage: Triangle inequality pruning and symmetric self-join filtering in DuckDB.
sql:
-- Detect duplicate ticket pairs with cosine similarity >= 0.88
            SELECT 
                t1.ticket_id AS primary_ticket_id,
                t1.subject AS primary_subject,
                t2.ticket_id AS duplicate_ticket_id,
                t2.subject AS duplicate_subject,
                ROUND(array_cosine_similarity(t1.vector, t2.vector), 4) AS similarity
            FROM support_tickets t1
            JOIN support_tickets t2 
              ON t1.ticket_id < t2.ticket_id -- strictly upper triangle to avoid duplicates and self-matching
             AND array_cosine_similarity(t1.vector, t2.vector) >= 0.88
            ORDER BY similarity DESC;

title: Multi-Merchant Near-Duplicate Catalog Resolution with Price Consistency
human_context: Marketplaces aggregate catalogs from thousands of sellers. Matching identical items requires high semantic vector similarity AND compatible price bounds (e.g. price within 20%).
hidden_trap: Vector similarity alone matches accessories to main products; price filtering alone matches unrelated items.
duckdb_advantage: DuckDB combines vector math and arithmetic bounds in a single joint execution predicate.
setup_sql:
CREATE TABLE merchant_catalog (
                sku_id INT,
                merchant VARCHAR,
                title VARCHAR,
                price DECIMAL(10,2),
                vector FLOAT[3]
            );
            INSERT INTO merchant_catalog VALUES
                (1, 'Merchant A', 'Sony WH-1000XM5 Noise-Cancelling Headphones', 349.99, [0.95, 0.1, 0.05]::FLOAT[3]),
                (2, 'Merchant B', 'Sony WH1000XM5 Wireless Headset - Black',     339.00, [0.94, 0.12, 0.04]::FLOAT[3]),
                (3, 'Merchant C', 'Sony Headphone Replacement Ear Cushions',       29.99, [0.88, 0.2, 0.1]::FLOAT[3]);
sql:
-- Match identical product listings across merchants (high similarity + price within 20%)
            SELECT 
                a.sku_id AS sku_a,
                a.merchant AS merchant_a,
                a.title AS title_a,
                b.sku_id AS sku_b,
                b.merchant AS merchant_b,
                b.title AS title_b,
                ROUND(array_cosine_similarity(a.vector, b.vector), 4) AS similarity,
                ROUND(ABS(a.price - b.price) / a.price * 100, 1) AS price_difference_pct
            FROM merchant_catalog a
            JOIN merchant_catalog b
              ON a.sku_id < b.sku_id
             AND a.merchant != b.merchant
             AND array_cosine_similarity(a.vector, b.vector) >= 0.90
             AND ABS(a.price - b.price) <= (0.20 * a.price)
            ORDER BY similarity DESC;

title: ColBERT Multi-Vector Late Interaction (MaxSim) in Pure SQL
human_context: Advanced retrieval models (ColBERT / Sanity) represent queries and documents as collections of token vectors. Scoring computes MaxSim: for each query token, take the maximum cosine similarity across all document tokens, then sum.
hidden_trap: Implementing late interaction typically requires specialized Python tensor pipelines.
duckdb_advantage: DuckDB can compute multi-vector token interactions, grouping by query token and document ID in vectorized SQL.
sql:
-- ColBERT MaxSim calculation: SUM_q( MAX_d( sim(q, d) ) )
            WITH token_sims AS (
                SELECT 
                    q.q_token_id,
                    q.token_text AS q_token,
                    d.doc_id,
                    d.token_text AS d_token,
                    array_cosine_similarity(q.vec, d.vec) AS sim
                FROM query_tokens q
                CROSS JOIN doc_token_embeddings d
            ),
            max_sim_per_query_token AS (
                SELECT 
                    doc_id,
                    q_token_id,
                    MAX(sim) AS max_token_sim
                FROM token_sims
                GROUP BY doc_id, q_token_id
            )
            SELECT 
                doc_id,
                ROUND(SUM(max_token_sim), 4) AS colbert_maxsim_score
            FROM max_sim_per_query_token
            GROUP BY doc_id
            ORDER BY colbert_maxsim_score DESC;

title: User Profile Preference Vector Centroid Aggregation
human_context: To personalize feeds, recommendation engines compute a dynamic user preference vector by calculating the average centroid of the embeddings of products the user clicked in the last 7 days.
hidden_trap: SQL standard lacks native array averaging; unnesting arrays without proper positional indexes scrambles vector dimensions.
duckdb_advantage: DuckDB array indexing and UNNEST WITH ORDINALITY allow dimension-wise vector averaging.
sql:
-- Calculate element-wise centroid vector for user 42
            WITH unnested_dims AS (
                SELECT 
                    user_id,
                    item_id,
                    UNNEST(item_vector) AS val,
                    GENERATE_SUBSCRIPTS(item_vector, 1) AS dim_idx
                FROM user_clicks_vectors
            ),
            avg_dims AS (
                SELECT 
                    user_id,
                    dim_idx,
                    ROUND(AVG(val), 4) AS avg_dim_val
                FROM unnested_dims
                GROUP BY user_id, dim_idx
                ORDER BY user_id, dim_idx
            )
            SELECT 
                user_id,
                LIST(avg_dim_val)::FLOAT[3] AS user_preference_centroid
            FROM avg_dims
            GROUP BY user_id;

title: K-Means Clustering Assignment and Centroid Update in Pure SQL
human_context: Unsupervised customer segmentation can be run directly inside DuckDB by assigning customer vectors to the nearest centroid and recomputing cluster means in a single query.
hidden_trap: Running ML clustering outside the warehouse requires exporting millions of vectors over the network.
duckdb_advantage: DuckDB computes distance matrices and partition centroids natively at memory bandwidth speeds.
sql:
-- Step 1: Assign each point to the closest cluster centroid via array_distance
            WITH point_distances AS (
                SELECT 
                    p.point_id,
                    p.coord,
                    c.cluster_id,
                    array_distance(p.coord, c.center) AS dist,
                    ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY p.point_id ORDER BY array_distance(p.coord, c.center) ASC) AS rank_closest
                FROM data_points p
                CROSS JOIN cluster_centroids c
            )
            SELECT 
                point_id,
                cluster_id AS assigned_cluster,
                ROUND(dist, 4) AS distance_to_center
            FROM point_distances
            WHERE rank_closest = 1
            ORDER BY point_id;

title: Vector Anomaly Detection via Average K-Nearest Neighbor Distance
human_context: Anomalous sensor readings or fraudulent transaction vectors reside in sparse regions of the embedding space. Measuring the average distance to a vector's 3 nearest neighbors flags outliers.
hidden_trap: Setting a global static distance threshold fails when data clusters have variable local densities.
duckdb_advantage: DuckDB window functions compute localized k-NN distances per entity without external libraries.
sql:
-- Calculate average distance to 2 nearest neighbors to score anomaly level
            WITH pairwise_distances AS (
                SELECT 
                    a.tx_id,
                    b.tx_id AS neighbor_id,
                    array_distance(a.vec, b.vec) AS dist,
                    ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY a.tx_id ORDER BY array_distance(a.vec, b.vec) ASC) AS k_rank
                FROM transaction_embeddings a
                JOIN transaction_embeddings b ON a.tx_id != b.tx_id
            ),
            knn_avg AS (
                SELECT 
                    tx_id,
                    AVG(dist) AS mean_2nn_distance
                FROM pairwise_distances
                WHERE k_rank <= 2
                GROUP BY tx_id
            )
            SELECT 
                tx_id,
                ROUND(mean_2nn_distance, 4) AS outlier_score,
                CASE WHEN mean_2nn_distance > 5.0 THEN 'ANOMALOUS_OUTLIER' ELSE 'NORMAL' END AS classification
            FROM knn_avg
            ORDER BY outlier_score DESC;

title: Cohort-Constrained Vector Match with Geographical Regionality
human_context: Real-world matchmaking (dating apps, gig-economy driver matching) requires vector personality/skill compatibility joined with strict relational geographic and category boundaries.
hidden_trap: Matching vectors globally without partitioning by region produces candidates located 3,000 miles away.
duckdb_advantage: DuckDB joins relational partitions (region = 'NA-WEST') directly with vector distance.
sql:
-- Match jobs to candidates strictly within matching geographical region ordered by skill compatibility
            SELECT 
                j.job_id,
                j.region,
                c.candidate_id,
                ROUND(array_cosine_similarity(c.skills_vec, j.required_vec), 4) AS skill_fit_score
            FROM job_openings j
            JOIN candidates c
              ON j.region = c.region
            ORDER BY skill_fit_score DESC;

title: Multi-Modal Joint Retrieval (Image + Text Query Embedding Fusion)
human_context: In e-commerce search, users submit a photo and a text clarification (e.g. photo of dress + 'in floral silk'). We compute a weighted combination of image-vector and text-vector similarity.
hidden_trap: Treating text and image vectors as independent queries yields conflicting rank lists.
duckdb_advantage: DuckDB can evaluate multiple vector distance functions in a single projection pass.
sql:
-- Joint multi-modal score: 60% image vector similarity + 40% text vector similarity
            SELECT 
                item_id,
                title,
                ROUND(array_cosine_similarity(img_vec, [0.82, 0.18]::FLOAT[2]), 4) AS img_sim,
                ROUND(array_cosine_similarity(txt_vec, [0.92, 0.08]::FLOAT[2]), 4) AS txt_sim,
                ROUND(
                    0.60 * array_cosine_similarity(img_vec, [0.82, 0.18]::FLOAT[2]) +
                    0.40 * array_cosine_similarity(txt_vec, [0.92, 0.08]::FLOAT[2]), 4
                ) AS joint_multimodal_score
            FROM fashion_items
            ORDER BY joint_multimodal_score DESC;

title: Maximal Marginal Relevance (MMR) Diversity Reranking in SQL
human_context: Standard vector retrieval often returns 5 virtually identical articles. MMR penalizes redundancy by selecting documents that are similar to the query but dissimilar to already-selected documents.
hidden_trap: Pure relevance search creates echo-chamber search results with zero content diversity.
duckdb_advantage: DuckDB can compute inter-candidate similarity matrix in memory to penalize redundancy.
setup_sql:
CREATE TABLE news_articles (
                article_id INT,
                headline VARCHAR,
                vec FLOAT[2]
            );
            INSERT INTO news_articles VALUES
                (1, 'Fed cuts interest rates by 25 bps',      [0.99, 0.05]::FLOAT[2]),
                (2, 'Central bank lowers benchmark 25 bps',   [0.98, 0.06]::FLOAT[2]), -- Redundant clone
                (3, 'Tech stock rally follows monetary shift', [0.80, 0.45]::FLOAT[2]); -- Diverse relevant
sql:
-- First candidate is highest query similarity; score subsequent candidates by query sim minus similarity to article 1
            WITH ranked_candidates AS (
                SELECT 
                    article_id,
                    headline,
                    vec,
                    array_cosine_similarity(vec, [1.0, 0.0]::FLOAT[2]) AS query_sim
                FROM news_articles
            )
            SELECT 
                c.article_id,
                c.headline,
                ROUND(c.query_sim, 4) AS query_relevance,
                ROUND(array_cosine_similarity(c.vec, top1.vec), 4) AS redundancy_with_top1,
                -- MMR formula: 0.7 * Sim(doc, query) - 0.3 * Sim(doc, top1)
                ROUND(0.7 * c.query_sim - 0.3 * array_cosine_similarity(c.vec, top1.vec), 4) AS mmr_score
            FROM ranked_candidates c
            CROSS JOIN (SELECT vec FROM ranked_candidates ORDER BY query_sim DESC LIMIT 1) top1
            ORDER BY mmr_score DESC;

title: Pairwise Vector Similarity Self-Join with Coarse Cluster Pruning
human_context: Finding all similar document pairs across 100,000 docs is O(N^2) (10 billion checks). Partitioning into coarse category buckets first reduces search to O(N * (N/K)).
hidden_trap: Unpartitioned cross joins cause out-of-memory crashes on analytical engines.
duckdb_advantage: DuckDB evaluates equi-join partition keys before computing array_cosine_similarity.
sql:
-- Pairwise similarity evaluated ONLY within shared bucket partitions
            SELECT 
                a.doc_id AS doc_a,
                b.doc_id AS doc_b,
                a.bucket_id,
                ROUND(array_cosine_similarity(a.vector, b.vector), 4) AS similarity
            FROM corpus a
            JOIN corpus b
              ON a.bucket_id = b.bucket_id
             AND a.doc_id < b.doc_id
            WHERE array_cosine_similarity(a.vector, b.vector) >= 0.85
            ORDER BY similarity DESC;

title: Latent Factor Matrix Factorization Dot Product Recommendation
human_context: Matrix factorization (SVD / ALS) maps users and movies to latent factor vectors. Predicted rating is dot product of user vector and movie vector plus user and movie bias terms.
hidden_trap: Omitting bias terms causes popular movies to be underrated and niche items to be overrated.
duckdb_advantage: DuckDB can evaluate latent factor dot products combined with additive scalar bias terms.
sql:
-- Predict user rating: baseline (3.5) + u_bias + m_bias + (u_vec . m_vec)
            SELECT 
                u.user_id,
                m.movie_id,
                m.title,
                ROUND(
                    3.5 + u.user_bias + m.movie_bias + array_inner_product(u.u_vec, m.m_vec), 2
                ) AS predicted_rating
            FROM user_latent u
            CROSS JOIN item_latent m
            WHERE u.user_id = 1
            ORDER BY predicted_rating DESC;

title: Vector Repulsion Scoring (Positive vs Negative Query Guidance)
human_context: In image generation and semantic search, users supply positive and negative prompts (e.g. 'cyberpunk city' NOT 'blurry / low quality'). The score boosts positive similarity and penalizes negative similarity.
hidden_trap: Filtering out negatives with boolean NOT drops items that have even slight overlap with negative words.
duckdb_advantage: DuckDB computes continuous vector repulsion formulas in standard SQL expressions.
sql:
-- Positive query: [1.0, 0.0] (cyberpunk neon), Negative query: [0.0, 1.0] (blurry/rustic)
            -- Net Score = Cosine(vec, pos) - (0.5 * Cosine(vec, neg))
            SELECT 
                asset_id,
                name,
                ROUND(array_cosine_similarity(vec, [1.0, 0.0]::FLOAT[2]), 4) AS pos_sim,
                ROUND(array_cosine_similarity(vec, [0.0, 1.0]::FLOAT[2]), 4) AS neg_sim,
                ROUND(
                    array_cosine_similarity(vec, [1.0, 0.0]::FLOAT[2]) - 
                    (0.50 * array_cosine_similarity(vec, [0.0, 1.0]::FLOAT[2])), 4
                ) AS net_guided_score
            FROM generative_assets
            ORDER BY net_guided_score DESC;

title: Document-Level Aggregation with Best-Chunk Pooling in RAG
human_context: Long PDF manuals are split into 50 chunks each. To avoid returning 5 chunks from the exact same PDF manual, we retrieve the best chunk per document and aggregate at the document level.
hidden_trap: Returning raw chunk Top-K dominates the context window with duplicates from a single document.
duckdb_advantage: DuckDB QUALIFY clause filters for the top chunk per document without nested CTEs.
setup_sql:
CREATE TABLE document_chunks (
                chunk_id INT,
                doc_id INT,
                doc_title VARCHAR,
                chunk_text VARCHAR,
                vec FLOAT[2]
            );
            INSERT INTO document_chunks VALUES
                (101, 1, 'Manual A', 'Setup guide section 1', [0.95, 0.1]::FLOAT[2]),
                (102, 1, 'Manual A', 'Setup guide section 2', [0.92, 0.15]::FLOAT[2]),
                (103, 2, 'Manual B', 'Troubleshooting section 1', [0.88, 0.2]::FLOAT[2]);
sql:
-- Retrieve the single highest-scoring chunk per document using QUALIFY
            SELECT 
                doc_id,
                doc_title,
                chunk_id,
                chunk_text,
                ROUND(array_cosine_similarity(vec, [1.0, 0.0]::FLOAT[2]), 4) AS chunk_score
            FROM document_chunks
            QUALIFY ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
                PARTITION BY doc_id 
                ORDER BY array_cosine_similarity(vec, [1.0, 0.0]::FLOAT[2]) DESC
            ) = 1
            ORDER BY chunk_score DESC;

title: Dynamic Context Window Token Budget Packing for LLM RAG
human_context: When assembling retrieved chunks for an LLM prompt, you have a strict token limit (e.g. 1,000 tokens). You must greedily pick highest-similarity chunks until the cumulative token sum would exceed the budget.
hidden_trap: Picking a fixed LIMIT 10 can overflow LLM token limits or waste available prompt capacity.
duckdb_advantage: DuckDB cumulative window sums (`SUM(token_count) OVER (...)`) cleanly enforce strict budgets.
setup_sql:
CREATE TABLE rag_candidate_chunks (
                chunk_id INT,
                token_count INT,
                vec FLOAT[2]
            );
            INSERT INTO rag_candidate_chunks VALUES
                (1, 400, [0.95, 0.05]::FLOAT[2]),
                (2, 350, [0.90, 0.10]::FLOAT[2]),
                (3, 400, [0.85, 0.15]::FLOAT[2]); -- Exceeds 1000 total budget
sql:
-- Greedily pack chunks ordered by similarity up to strict 1,000 token budget
            WITH ranked_chunks AS (
                SELECT 
                    chunk_id,
                    token_count,
                    array_cosine_similarity(vec, [1.0, 0.0]::FLOAT[2]) AS score,
                    SUM(token_count) OVER (
                        ORDER BY array_cosine_similarity(vec, [1.0, 0.0]::FLOAT[2]) DESC
                    ) AS cumulative_tokens
                FROM rag_candidate_chunks
            )
            SELECT 
                chunk_id,
                token_count,
                cumulative_tokens,
                ROUND(score, 4) AS similarity_score
            FROM ranked_chunks
            WHERE cumulative_tokens <= 1000
            ORDER BY similarity_score DESC;

title: Two-Stage Retrieval: Bi-Encoder Candidate Generation for Re-ranking
human_context: Modern enterprise search uses a 2-stage pipeline: Fast bi-encoder vector search retrieves Top-50 candidates, which are then passed to a computationally heavy cross-encoder for final scoring.
hidden_trap: Running heavy cross-encoder models across entire datasets is computationally impossible.
duckdb_advantage: DuckDB can quickly filter millions of rows down to 50 candidates in milliseconds.
sql:
-- First-stage candidate extraction: Top candidates in relevant category
            SELECT 
                article_id,
                category,
                ROUND(array_cosine_similarity(vec, [0.95, 0.05]::FLOAT[2]), 4) AS stage1_biencoder_score
            FROM knowledge_articles
            WHERE category = 'tech'
            ORDER BY stage1_biencoder_score DESC
            LIMIT 50;

title: Temporal Semantic Drift Tracking across Document Embedding Centroids
human_context: As companies evolve, the meaning of terms like 'security' or 'remote work' shifts. Tracking the cosine distance between monthly embedding centroids reveals semantic concept drift.
hidden_trap: Ignoring semantic drift causes older documentation to silently diverge from current employee search queries.
duckdb_advantage: DuckDB calculates monthly vector centroids and inter-month drift using LAG.
setup_sql:
CREATE TABLE monthly_centroids (
                month_date DATE,
                centroid FLOAT[2]
            );
            INSERT INTO monthly_centroids VALUES
                ('2026-01-01', [0.90, 0.10]::FLOAT[2]),
                ('2026-02-01', [0.88, 0.12]::FLOAT[2]),
                ('2026-03-01', [0.70, 0.35]::FLOAT[2]); -- Significant semantic drift
sql:
-- Track month-over-month semantic drift in concept centroids
            SELECT 
                month_date,
                centroid,
                LAG(centroid) OVER (ORDER BY month_date) AS prev_month_centroid,
                ROUND(
                    1.0 - array_cosine_similarity(
                        centroid, 
                        LAG(centroid) OVER (ORDER BY month_date)
                    ), 4
                ) AS drift_distance_from_prev_month
            FROM monthly_centroids
            ORDER BY month_date;

title: Hierarchical Coarse-to-Fine Multi-Level Vector Filtering
human_context: In massive enterprise catalogs, searching 100 million items is accelerated by first matching high-level department embedding centroids, then searching specific item vectors inside matching departments.
hidden_trap: Flat brute-force vector search over hundreds of millions of items consumes excessive compute.
duckdb_advantage: DuckDB joins coarse department vectors directly to fine item vectors in a single query.
sql:
-- Find best matching department, then retrieve top items strictly within that department
            WITH top_dept AS (
                SELECT dept_id
                FROM departments
                ORDER BY array_cosine_similarity(dept_centroid, [0.95, 0.05]::FLOAT[2]) DESC
                LIMIT 1
            )
            SELECT 
                i.item_id,
                i.item_name,
                ROUND(array_cosine_similarity(i.item_vector, [0.95, 0.05]::FLOAT[2]), 4) AS fine_sim_score
            FROM items i
            JOIN top_dept d ON i.dept_id = d.dept_id
            ORDER BY fine_sim_score DESC;

title: Vector Quantization Precision Distortion & Reconstruction Error
human_context: To compress embeddings from 32-bit floats to 8-bit integers, engineers evaluate the reconstruction error (distance between uncompressed and quantized vector) to measure fidelity loss.
hidden_trap: Deploying quantized embeddings without evaluating distortion leads to silent degradation in search accuracy.
duckdb_advantage: DuckDB can evaluate floating-point vector distances against quantized projections.
sql:
-- Evaluate Euclidean distortion and cosine fidelity loss per vector
            SELECT 
                vector_id,
                ROUND(array_distance(fp32_vec, quantized_vec), 6) AS l2_quantization_error,
                ROUND(1.0 - array_cosine_similarity(fp32_vec, quantized_vec), 6) AS cosine_distortion
            FROM vector_compression_test
            ORDER BY l2_quantization_error DESC;

title: Zero-Shot Query Intent Classification via Prototype Vector Distance
human_context: Instead of training a BERT classifier, user query vectors are compared against pre-computed 'intent prototype vectors' (e.g. Navigational, Transactional, Informational). The closest prototype labels the query intent.
hidden_trap: Maintaining external classifier microservices adds 50ms latency to query planning.
duckdb_advantage: DuckDB classifies intent in pure SQL with sub-millisecond execution.
sql:
-- Classify each query to its closest intent prototype
            WITH ranked_intents AS (
                SELECT 
                    q.query_id,
                    q.query_text,
                    p.intent_name,
                    array_cosine_similarity(q.query_vector, p.prototype_vector) AS intent_similarity,
                    ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
                        PARTITION BY q.query_id 
                        ORDER BY array_cosine_similarity(q.query_vector, p.prototype_vector) DESC
                    ) AS rank_match
                FROM inbound_queries q
                CROSS JOIN intent_prototypes p
            )
            SELECT 
                query_id,
                query_text,
                intent_name AS predicted_intent,
                ROUND(intent_similarity, 4) AS confidence
            FROM ranked_intents
            WHERE rank_match = 1
            ORDER BY query_id;

title: Contrastive Triplet Evaluation: Anchor-Positive-Negative Separation
human_context: In embedding model evaluation, high-quality models satisfy the triplet condition: distance(anchor, positive) + margin < distance(anchor, negative). We evaluate model margin violations directly in SQL.
hidden_trap: Validating embedding models often requires ad-hoc PyTorch scripts; SQL evaluation enables continuous monitoring in production.
duckdb_advantage: DuckDB computes margin violations across millions of triplets in seconds.
setup_sql:
CREATE TABLE eval_triplets (
                triplet_id INT,
                anchor_vec FLOAT[2],
                positive_vec FLOAT[2],
                negative_vec FLOAT[2]
            );
            INSERT INTO eval_triplets VALUES
                -- Good triplet: pos is close, neg is far
                (1, [1.0, 0.0]::FLOAT[2], [0.95, 0.05]::FLOAT[2], [0.1, 0.9]::FLOAT[2]),
                -- Violated triplet: neg is closer than pos!
                (2, [1.0, 0.0]::FLOAT[2], [0.5, 0.5]::FLOAT[2],   [0.9, 0.1]::FLOAT[2]);
sql:
-- Compute triplet margin violation with margin = 0.2
            -- Violation = GREATEST(0, dist(a, p) - dist(a, n) + margin)
            SELECT 
                triplet_id,
                ROUND(array_distance(anchor_vec, positive_vec), 4) AS dist_pos,
                ROUND(array_distance(anchor_vec, negative_vec), 4) AS dist_neg,
                ROUND(
                    GREATEST(0.0, array_distance(anchor_vec, positive_vec) - array_distance(anchor_vec, negative_vec) + 0.20), 4
                ) AS triplet_margin_loss,
                CASE 
                    WHEN (array_distance(anchor_vec, positive_vec) - array_distance(anchor_vec, negative_vec) + 0.20) > 0 
                    THEN 'VIOLATION' 
                    ELSE 'SATISFIED' 
                END AS evaluation_status
            FROM eval_triplets
            ORDER BY triplet_id;

title: DuckDB Full-Text Search (FTS) BM25 Term Relevance Scoring
human_context: Traditional databases use simple `LIKE '%search%'` which treats 1 mention the same as 10 mentions and ignores document frequency. BM25 scores term saturation and document rarity.
hidden_trap: ILIKE matches substrings blindly (e.g. 'cat' matches 'scattered' or 'certificate') with zero relevancy ranking.
duckdb_advantage: DuckDB has native full-text indexing via the `fts` extension (`PRAGMA create_fts_index` and `match_bm25`).
sql:
-- BM25 full-text search for 'analytical database'
            WITH scored_articles AS (
                SELECT 
                    doc_id,
                    title,
                    body,
                    fts_main_articles.match_bm25(doc_id, 'analytical database') AS bm25_score
                FROM articles
            )
            SELECT 
                doc_id,
                title,
                ROUND(bm25_score, 4) AS bm25_score
            FROM scored_articles
            WHERE bm25_score IS NOT NULL
            ORDER BY bm25_score DESC;

title: Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF) Hybrid Search (BM25 + Dense Vectors)
human_context: Hybrid search combines sparse keyword search (great for exact names and acronyms) with dense vector search (great for synonyms and concepts). RRF merges both rank lists using: RRF_score = 1/(60 + rank_bm25) + 1/(60 + rank_vec).
hidden_trap: Adding raw BM25 scores (range 0 to 50+) directly to cosine similarity scores (range 0 to 1) allows BM25 to completely drown out vector relevance.
duckdb_advantage: DuckDB window functions compute dense ranks across both retrieval channels and fuse them in a single query.
sql:
-- Hybrid RRF rank fusion between BM25 lexical score and dense vector cosine similarity
            WITH ranked_lexical AS (
                SELECT 
                    doc_id,
                    title,
                    ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY lexical_score DESC) AS rank_lexical
                FROM corpus_docs
            ),
            ranked_vector AS (
                SELECT 
                    doc_id,
                    title,
                    ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
                        ORDER BY array_cosine_similarity(vec, [1.0, 0.0]::FLOAT[2]) DESC
                    ) AS rank_vector
                FROM corpus_docs
            )
            SELECT 
                l.doc_id,
                l.title,
                l.rank_lexical,
                v.rank_vector,
                -- Standard RRF formula with k = 60
                ROUND((1.0 / (60.0 + l.rank_lexical)) + (1.0 / (60.0 + v.rank_vector)), 6) AS rrf_score
            FROM ranked_lexical l
            JOIN ranked_vector v ON l.doc_id = v.doc_id
            ORDER BY rrf_score DESC;

title: Min-Max Normalized Convex Combination Hybrid Search
human_context: An alternative to rank-based RRF is score-based fusion: min-max scale lexical scores to [0, 1] and vector scores to [0, 1], then take alpha * lexical + (1 - alpha) * vector.
hidden_trap: Division by zero when all scores in a small result set are identical.
duckdb_advantage: DuckDB NULLIF and window MIN/MAX cleanly handle degenerate score distributions.
sql:
-- Min-Max normalization and 50/50 convex combination
            WITH bounds AS (
                SELECT 
                    doc_id,
                    title,
                    raw_bm25,
                    vector_sim,
                    MIN(raw_bm25) OVER () AS min_bm25,
                    MAX(raw_bm25) OVER () AS max_bm25,
                    MIN(vector_sim) OVER () AS min_vec,
                    MAX(vector_sim) OVER () AS max_vec
                FROM search_candidates
            ),
            normalized AS (
                SELECT 
                    doc_id,
                    title,
                    COALESCE((raw_bm25 - min_bm25) / NULLIF(max_bm25 - min_bm25, 0), 1.0) AS norm_bm25,
                    COALESCE((vector_sim - min_vec) / NULLIF(max_vec - min_vec, 0), 1.0) AS norm_vec
                FROM bounds
            )
            SELECT 
                doc_id,
                title,
                ROUND(norm_bm25, 4) AS norm_bm25,
                ROUND(norm_vec, 4) AS norm_vec,
                ROUND(0.50 * norm_bm25 + 0.50 * norm_vec, 4) AS convex_hybrid_score
            FROM normalized
            ORDER BY convex_hybrid_score DESC;

title: Typo-Tolerant Search with Levenshtein Edit Distance & Length Bounds
human_context: Users frequently misspell search terms (e.g. 'postgre' -> 'postgresql'). Levenshtein distance counts insertions, deletions, and substitutions.
hidden_trap: Computing Levenshtein distance on every catalog word is CPU intensive without pre-filtering on string length (ABS(len_a - len_b) <= max_distance).
duckdb_advantage: DuckDB pushes string length checks ahead of native `levenshtein()` evaluations.
sql:
-- Find keywords within edit distance <= 2 of search query 'posgresql'
            SELECT 
                keyword_id,
                keyword,
                levenshtein(keyword, 'posgresql') AS edit_distance
            FROM catalog_keywords
            -- Pre-filter: word length cannot differ by more than max allowed edit distance (2)
            WHERE ABS(LENGTH(keyword) - LENGTH('posgresql')) <= 2
              AND levenshtein(keyword, 'posgresql') <= 2
            ORDER BY edit_distance ASC;

title: Brand & Name Fuzzy Search via Jaro-Winkler Prefix Similarity
human_context: In e-commerce, users often mistype the suffixes of brand names ('Samsumg' vs 'Samsung'). Jaro-Winkler gives higher weight to prefix matches, making it ideal for proper names.
hidden_trap: Standard Levenshtein treats mistakes at the start of a word the same as at the end.
duckdb_advantage: DuckDB includes native `jaro_winkler_similarity(a, b)` returning normalized [0, 1] scores.
sql:
-- Match brand query 'Samsun' with threshold >= 0.85
            SELECT 
                brand_id,
                brand_name,
                ROUND(jaro_winkler_similarity(brand_name, 'Samsun'), 4) AS jaro_similarity
            FROM brands
            WHERE jaro_winkler_similarity(brand_name, 'Samsun') >= 0.85
            ORDER BY jaro_similarity DESC;

title: Multi-Field Weighted Full-Text Retrieval (Title 3x, Body 1x)
human_context: A match in a document title or product headline is far more indicative of relevance than a passing mention in the body text.
hidden_trap: Concatenating title and body into a single column gives equal weight to all words.
duckdb_advantage: DuckDB can evaluate independent field matches and combine them with linear weighting in SQL.
sql:
-- Search for 'wireless headphones': Title matches weighted 3.0x, Body matches weighted 1.0x
