            WITH scored AS (
                SELECT 
                    post_id,
                    title,
                    ROUND(
                        (CASE WHEN title ILIKE '%wireless%' THEN 3.0 ELSE 0.0 END) +
                        (CASE WHEN title ILIKE '%headphones%' THEN 3.0 ELSE 0.0 END) +
                        (CASE WHEN body ILIKE '%wireless%' THEN 1.0 ELSE 0.0 END) +
                        (CASE WHEN body ILIKE '%headphones%' THEN 1.0 ELSE 0.0 END), 2
                    ) AS multi_field_score
                FROM product_posts
            )
            SELECT 
                post_id,
                title,
                multi_field_score
            FROM scored
            WHERE multi_field_score > 0
            ORDER BY multi_field_score DESC;

title: Exact Phrase Proximity Boosting in Keyword Retrieval
human_context: If a user searches for 'machine learning', an article containing the exact phrase 'machine learning' should rank higher than an article where 'machine' is in paragraph 1 and 'learning' is in paragraph 8.
hidden_trap: Pure bag-of-words keyword matches ignore token proximity and phrase boundaries.
duckdb_advantage: DuckDB combines exact phrase substring checks with token matching.
sql:
-- Query: 'machine' AND 'learning', with a 5.0x boost for exact phrase match
            SELECT 
                article_id,
                text_content,
                (CASE WHEN text_content ILIKE '%machine%' THEN 1.0 ELSE 0.0 END +
                 CASE WHEN text_content ILIKE '%learning%' THEN 1.0 ELSE 0.0 END +
                 CASE WHEN text_content ILIKE '%machine learning%' THEN 5.0 ELSE 0.0 END) AS relevance_score
            FROM articles_proximity
            WHERE text_content ILIKE '%machine%' AND text_content ILIKE '%learning%'
            ORDER BY relevance_score DESC;

title: Stopword Filtering and Query Token Cleansing in SQL
human_context: Search queries like 'what is the best laptop' contain stop words ('what', 'is', 'the') that dilute search precision if not filtered prior to catalog matching.
hidden_trap: Leaving stopwords in keyword queries causes high-frequency words to trigger millions of false positive matches.
duckdb_advantage: DuckDB array functions (`list_filter`) can cleanse query tokens against stopword tables.
setup_sql:
CREATE TABLE stopwords (word VARCHAR);
            INSERT INTO stopwords VALUES ('what'), ('is'), ('the'), ('and'), ('or'), ('a'), ('an');
sql:
-- Cleanse raw search tokens by filtering out stopwords
            WITH raw_query AS (
                SELECT UNNEST(string_split(lower('what is the best gaming laptop'), ' ')) AS token
            ),
            clean_tokens AS (
                SELECT q.token
                FROM raw_query q
                LEFT JOIN stopwords s ON q.token = s.word
                WHERE s.word IS NULL
            )
            SELECT 
                list(token) AS clean_tokens,
                string_agg(token, ' ') AS cleansed_search_query
            FROM clean_tokens;

title: Faceted Search Aggregations over Semi-Structured JSON Attributes
human_context: When a customer searches for 'laptops', e-commerce search engines return matching items along with dynamic facet counts (e.g. Brand: Apple (12), Dell (8); RAM: 16GB (15), 32GB (5)) extracted from JSON specs.
hidden_trap: Running separate queries for each facet dimension multiplies query latency and database load.
duckdb_advantage: DuckDB extracts JSON paths (`->>`) and aggregates multiple facet dimensions in parallel.
sql:
-- Extract faceted breakdown of matching laptop brands and RAM capacities
            WITH matching_items AS (
                SELECT 
                    item_id,
                    title,
                    specs->>'brand' AS brand,
                    specs->>'ram' AS ram
                FROM electronics_catalog
            )
            SELECT 
                'brand' AS facet_dimension,
                brand AS facet_value,
                COUNT(*) AS match_count
            FROM matching_items
            GROUP BY brand
            UNION ALL
            SELECT 
                'ram' AS facet_dimension,
                ram AS facet_value,
                COUNT(*) AS match_count
            FROM matching_items
            GROUP BY ram
            ORDER BY facet_dimension, match_count DESC, facet_value ASC;

title: Trigram / N-Gram Token Substring Matching for Technical Error Logs
human_context: In observability platforms (Datadog, Splunk), engineers search stack traces with partial error signatures. Trigram decomposition enables robust partial substring index matching.
hidden_trap: Full regex evaluations on raw million-line log tables trigger catastrophic backtracking.
duckdb_advantage: DuckDB n-gram tokenization and array overlaps provide fast log signature matching.
sql:
-- Find logs matching 'NullPointer' or 'OutOfMemory' error signatures
            SELECT 
                log_id,
                error_message,
                CASE 
                    WHEN error_message LIKE '%NullPointer%' THEN 'NPE_EXCEPTION'
                    WHEN error_message LIKE '%OutOfMemory%' THEN 'OOM_KILL'
                    ELSE 'OTHER'
                END AS classified_signature
            FROM incident_logs
            WHERE error_message LIKE '%NullPointer%' 
               OR error_message LIKE '%OutOfMemory%'
            ORDER BY log_id;

title: Dynamic Query Synonym Expansion via Relational Thesaurus
human_context: When a customer searches for 'sofa', they also expect to see listings titled 'couch' or 'settee'. Expanding queries using a synonym thesaurus bridges terminology gaps.
hidden_trap: Hardcoding synonyms into client-side application code makes vocabulary updates inflexible.
duckdb_advantage: DuckDB joins query tokens to relational synonym tables to score documents with expanded terms.
sql:
-- Expand search term 'sofa' with all relational synonyms and match inventory
            WITH expanded_terms AS (
                SELECT 'sofa' AS search_term
                UNION
                SELECT synonym FROM synonym_thesaurus WHERE base_term = 'sofa'
            )
            SELECT 
                f.item_id,
                f.description,
                t.search_term AS matched_alias
            FROM furniture_items f
            JOIN expanded_terms t 
              ON f.description ILIKE ('%' || t.search_term || '%')
            ORDER BY f.item_id;

title: Search Autocomplete Suggestion with Popularity Frequency Weighting
human_context: As users type 'air...', instant search suggests 'air fryer' (100k searches) before 'air mattress' (5k searches). Suggestions must match the prefix AND rank by historical popularity.
hidden_trap: Alphabetical sorting of prefix matches suggests obscure terms before popular items.
duckdb_advantage: DuckDB prefix filtering (`prefix_query || '%'`) combined with ordering indices produces sub-millisecond suggestions.
sql:
-- Autocomplete suggestions for prefix 'air' ranked by volume * conversion
            SELECT 
                query_string,
                monthly_search_volume,
                ROUND(monthly_search_volume * conversion_rate, 0) AS popularity_rank_score
            FROM search_telemetry
            WHERE query_string LIKE 'air%'
            ORDER BY popularity_rank_score DESC
            LIMIT 3;

title: High-Precision Boolean Search with Negation and Grouping
human_context: Legal e-discovery and patent search rely on exact Boolean syntax: (patent AND battery) NOT (lithium OR phone). Negations must be strictly applied without dropping valid candidate documents.
hidden_trap: Poor operator precedence in SQL boolean expressions causes negated terms to drop unrelated valid results.
duckdb_advantage: DuckDB SQL evaluates complex parenthesized boolean criteria with index acceleration.
sql:
-- Query: ('battery') AND NOT ('lithium' OR 'phone')
            SELECT 
                patent_id,
                abstract
            FROM patent_corpus
            WHERE abstract ILIKE '%battery%'
              AND NOT (abstract ILIKE '%lithium%' OR abstract ILIKE '%phone%')
            ORDER BY patent_id;

title: TF-IDF (Term Frequency - Inverse Document Frequency) in Pure SQL
human_context: TF-IDF is the foundational algorithm of information retrieval. Calculating it directly in SQL provides deep insight into term uniqueness across a corpus without requiring Python.
hidden_trap: Calculating document frequency across millions of documents requires careful window partitioning to avoid Cartesian explosions.
duckdb_advantage: DuckDB window functions compute corpus document counts (N) and term frequencies in parallel.
sql:
-- Calculate TF-IDF for term 'columnar' across 3 documents
            -- TF = term_count / total_terms_in_doc, IDF = LN(Total_Docs / Docs_With_Term)
            WITH doc_lengths AS (
                SELECT doc_id, SUM(term_count) AS doc_len
                FROM doc_words
                GROUP BY doc_id
            ),
            corpus_stats AS (
                SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT doc_id) AS total_docs FROM doc_words
            ),
            term_docs AS (
                SELECT term, COUNT(DISTINCT doc_id) AS docs_with_term
                FROM doc_words
                GROUP BY term
            )
            SELECT 
                w.doc_id,
                w.term,
                w.term_count,
                ROUND(w.term_count * 1.0 / l.doc_len, 4) AS tf,
                ROUND(LN(c.total_docs * 1.0 / td.docs_with_term), 4) AS idf,
                ROUND((w.term_count * 1.0 / l.doc_len) * LN(c.total_docs * 1.0 / td.docs_with_term), 4) AS tfidf_score
            FROM doc_words w
            JOIN doc_lengths l ON w.doc_id = l.doc_id
            JOIN term_docs td ON w.term = td.term
            CROSS JOIN corpus_stats c
            WHERE w.term = 'columnar'
            ORDER BY tfidf_score DESC;

title: Discounted Cumulative Gain (DCG) with Search Position Bias Discount
human_context: Users are far more likely to click the #1 search result than the #5 result regardless of relevance. Ranking quality is measured via Discounted Cumulative Gain: DCG = SUM(relevance / log2(rank + 1)).
hidden_trap: Simple click counts reward poorly placed relevant items unfairly.
duckdb_advantage: DuckDB math functions (`LOG2`) compute logarithmic rank discounts in vectorized window expressions.
setup_sql:
CREATE TABLE search_impressions (
                query_id INT,
                rank_position INT,
                relevance_label INT -- 0=irrelevant, 1=relevant, 2=perfect
            );
            INSERT INTO search_impressions VALUES
                (1, 1, 2), -- Rank 1: perfect match
                (1, 2, 0), -- Rank 2: bad match
                (1, 3, 1); -- Rank 3: good match
sql:
-- Calculate DCG@3 for query 1
            SELECT 
                query_id,
                ROUND(SUM(relevance_label / LOG2(rank_position + 1)), 4) AS dcg_at_3
            FROM search_impressions
            WHERE rank_position <= 3
            GROUP BY query_id;

title: Alphanumeric SKU Matching with Punctuation & Case Invariance
human_context: Customers search for model numbers in messy formats: 'wh-1000xm5', 'WH1000-XM5', 'wh 1000 xm5'. Robust search normalizes punctuation and whitespace before matching.
hidden_trap: Exact string equality misses 90% of technical product searches due to hyphens and spaces.
duckdb_advantage: DuckDB `regexp_replace` cleanses alphanumeric identifiers efficiently.
sql:
-- Cleanse search query 'wh1000xm5b' by stripping non-alphanumeric characters
            SELECT 
                sku_id,
                raw_sku,
                product_title
            FROM inventory_skus
            WHERE lower(regexp_replace(raw_sku, '[^a-zA-Z0-9]', '', 'g')) = lower(regexp_replace('wh 1000-xm5/b', '[^a-zA-Z0-9]', '', 'g'));

title: Dynamic Negative Keyword Exclusion in E-Commerce Filters
human_context: A user searches 'monitor -curved' to find flat computer monitors. The engine must extract positive search terms and suppress any record containing the negative terms.
hidden_trap: Negative keywords must not exclude items where the negative term appears with negation qualifiers (e.g. 'not curved').
duckdb_advantage: DuckDB regex matching and exclusion conditions execute in a single scan.
sql:
-- Positive term: 'monitor', Negative term: 'curved'
            SELECT 
                item_id,
                title,
                description
            FROM display_items
            WHERE (title ILIKE '%monitor%' OR description ILIKE '%monitor%')
              AND NOT (title ILIKE '%curved%' OR description ILIKE '%curved%')
            ORDER BY item_id;

title: Multi-Lingual Catalog Routing by Detected ISO Language Code
human_context: Global portals store titles in multiple localized columns (title_en, title_es, title_fr). Queries are dynamically routed to the matching language column based on user locale.
hidden_trap: Searching across all language columns simultaneously creates false-positive matches due to inter-language false cognates.
duckdb_advantage: DuckDB CASE projections route predicates to target language fields with zero query recompilation.
sql:
-- Match Spanish query 'Bicicleta' routed dynamically to title_es
            SELECT 
                product_id,
                title_es AS matched_title,
                'es' AS language_used
            FROM localized_products
            WHERE title_es ILIKE '%Bicicleta%'
            ORDER BY product_id;

title: Zero-Result Search Query Relaxation (Strict AND -> Loose OR Fallback)
human_context: If a multi-word search query (e.g. 'ergonomic mechanical wireless split keyboard') returns zero results under strict AND matching, modern engines gracefully relax to OR matching.
hidden_trap: Failing to return fallback results leads to user bounce and abandoned sessions.
duckdb_advantage: DuckDB CTEs can check candidate counts and conditionally branch to relaxed OR queries.
sql:
-- Query tokens: 'ergonomic', 'mechanical', 'wireless'
            WITH scored_matches AS (
                SELECT 
                    id,
                    title,
                    (CASE WHEN title ILIKE '%ergonomic%' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END +
                     CASE WHEN title ILIKE '%mechanical%' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END +
                     CASE WHEN title ILIKE '%wireless%' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS match_score
                FROM keyboard_catalog
            )
            SELECT 
                id,
                title,
                match_score,
                CASE WHEN match_score = 3 THEN 'STRICT_ALL_MATCH' ELSE 'RELAXED_PARTIAL_MATCH' END AS match_tier
            FROM scored_matches
            WHERE match_score >= 1
            ORDER BY match_score DESC, id;

title: Search Snippet Extraction: Context Window Around Matching Terms
human_context: Search results show a preview snippet containing the searched keyword with 30 characters of surrounding context rather than the beginning of a 2,000-word article.
hidden_trap: Substring extraction crashes when matching keywords appear near the very beginning or end of the text.
duckdb_advantage: DuckDB `GREATEST` and `SUBSTRING` functions construct safe boundary-clipped preview snippets.
sql:
-- Extract 25-character window surrounding the word 'vectorized'
            SELECT 
                post_id,
                '...' || SUBSTRING(
                    content,
                    GREATEST(1, INSTR(lower(content), 'vectorized') - 15),
                    LENGTH('vectorized') + 30
                ) || '...' AS snippet_preview
            FROM blog_posts
            WHERE content ILIKE '%vectorized%';

title: Customer Search-to-Purchase Path Attribution (Session Query Lift)
human_context: E-commerce search product managers need to know which search queries drove actual revenue. We link search queries to checkout events within the same 30-minute session.
hidden_trap: Attributing purchases to search queries that occurred after the purchase order was placed.
duckdb_advantage: DuckDB temporal range joins ensure search queries precede the checkout timestamp.
sql:
-- Attribute purchase to the most recent search query prior to order
            SELECT 
                o.order_id,
                o.user_id,
                o.order_total,
                s.query_term AS attributing_search_query,
                s.searched_at,
                o.ordered_at
            FROM completed_orders o
            ASOF JOIN user_search_queries s
              ON o.user_id = s.user_id
             AND o.ordered_at >= s.searched_at
            ORDER BY o.order_id;

title: Fuzzy Customer Entity Resolution across Disparate Data Sources
human_context: Merging CRM and billing databases requires linking customers with slight name and address variations (e.g. 'Robert Smith, 123 Main St' vs 'Bob Smith, 123 Main Street').
hidden_trap: Pairwise fuzzy string matching over millions of records is computationally prohibitive without blocking/canopy clustering.
duckdb_advantage: DuckDB uses zip-code blocking keys before computing string similarity.
sql:
-- Entity resolution: Match records with identical zip code and Jaro-Winkler name similarity >= 0.80
            SELECT 
                c.crm_id,
                c.name AS crm_name,
                b.bill_id,
                b.name AS billing_name,
                c.zip_code,
                ROUND(jaro_winkler_similarity(c.name, b.name), 4) AS name_similarity
            FROM crm_records c
            JOIN billing_records b
              ON c.zip_code = b.zip_code
             AND jaro_winkler_similarity(c.name, b.name) >= 0.80
            ORDER BY name_similarity DESC;

title: Search Term Co-Occurrence Matrix (Market Basket of Search Queries)
human_context: To suggest related searches, engines analyze queries searched together in the same session (e.g. users searching 'monitor' also search 'hdmi cable' 42% of the time).
hidden_trap: Self-joining search sessions without ordering (`a.term < b.term`) doubles matrix size with duplicate reversed pairs.
duckdb_advantage: DuckDB computes symmetric co-occurrence frequencies in a single pass.
sql:
-- Find pairs of terms most frequently searched in the same user session
            SELECT 
                a.term AS term_a,
                b.term AS term_b,
                COUNT(*) AS cooccurrence_count
            FROM session_searches a
            JOIN session_searches b
              ON a.session_id = b.session_id
             AND a.term < b.term
            GROUP BY a.term, b.term
            ORDER BY cooccurrence_count DESC, term_a, term_b;

title: 'Did You Mean?' Query Spell-Correction Suggestion Engine
human_context: When a query produces few results, search engines recommend a spell-corrected candidate word from the catalog vocabulary that has the lowest edit distance and highest document frequency.
hidden_trap: Suggesting rare typos back to users rather than verified popular vocabulary terms.
duckdb_advantage: DuckDB joins dictionary terms, calculates edit distance, and ranks by frequency in one query.
sql:
-- Given misspelled query 'wireles', propose top dictionary replacement with edit distance <= 1
            SELECT 
                term AS suggested_correction,
                doc_frequency,
                levenshtein(term, 'wireles') AS edit_distance
            FROM dictionary_terms
            WHERE levenshtein(term, 'wireles') <= 2
            ORDER BY edit_distance ASC, doc_frequency DESC
            LIMIT 1;

title: Hybrid Search with Hard Categorical Filter & Soft Merchant Quality Boost
human_context: Top marketplaces enforce strict hard filters (in-stock, prime shipping) while soft-boosting items based on merchant review rating: final_score = text_relevance * (1.0 + 0.1 * merchant_rating).
hidden_trap: Hard-filtering by rating eliminates high-relevance new merchants with few reviews.
duckdb_advantage: DuckDB combines hard boolean filtering with continuous multiplicative rating boosts.
setup_sql:
CREATE TABLE merchant_inventory (
                item_id INT,
                category VARCHAR,
                title VARCHAR,
                merchant_rating DOUBLE,
                is_available BOOLEAN
            );
            INSERT INTO merchant_inventory VALUES
                (1, 'Audio', 'Pro Studio Monitor Headphones', 4.9, true),
                (2, 'Audio', 'Budget Studio Headphones',       3.8, true),
                (3, 'Audio', 'Discontinued Vintage Headphones', 4.8, false);
sql:
-- Search 'Headphones' in 'Audio': Hard filter available=true, soft-boost by merchant rating
            WITH text_matches AS (
                SELECT 
                    item_id,
                    title,
                    merchant_rating,
                    -- Base relevance score from keyword matches
                    (CASE WHEN title ILIKE '%studio%' THEN 2.0 ELSE 1.0 END) AS base_relevance
                FROM merchant_inventory
                WHERE category = 'Audio'
                  AND is_available = true
                  AND title ILIKE '%Headphones%'
            )
            SELECT 
                item_id,
                title,
                merchant_rating,
                base_relevance,
                ROUND(base_relevance * (1.0 + (merchant_rating / 5.0) * 0.50), 2) AS boosted_final_score
            FROM text_matches
            ORDER BY boosted_final_score DESC;

title: Hierarchical Bill of Materials (BOM) Cost Rollup via Recursive CTE
human_context: Manufacturing an electric vehicle requires thousands of nested parts (Car -> Battery Pack -> Cell Module -> Lithium Cathode). Calculating unit cost requires rolling up quantities across arbitrary depth levels.
hidden_trap: Fixed joins only support fixed depth hierarchies (e.g. 3 levels max). If an assembly has 6 levels, fixed joins miss the lowest-tier parts entirely.
duckdb_advantage: DuckDB executes `WITH RECURSIVE` queries in memory with zero row-materialization overhead.
setup_sql:
CREATE TABLE bom_parts (
                parent_part VARCHAR,
                child_part VARCHAR,
                quantity_needed INT,
                unit_cost DECIMAL(10,2)
            );
            INSERT INTO bom_parts VALUES
                ('EV_CAR', 'CHASSIS', 1, 5000.00),
                ('EV_CAR', 'BATTERY_PACK', 1, 0.00),
                ('BATTERY_PACK', 'BATTERY_MODULE', 4, 0.00),
                ('BATTERY_MODULE', 'LITHIUM_CELL', 100, 15.00);
sql:
-- Recursively expand BOM tree to compute total quantity of base components
            WITH RECURSIVE bom_tree AS (
                -- Anchor: Top-level components of EV_CAR
                SELECT 
                    parent_part,
                    child_part,
                    quantity_needed AS total_qty,
                    1 AS depth
                FROM bom_parts
                WHERE parent_part = 'EV_CAR'
                
                UNION ALL
                
                -- Recursive: Multiply quantity down the hierarchy tree
                SELECT 
                    t.child_part AS parent_part,
                    b.child_part,
                    t.total_qty * b.quantity_needed AS total_qty,
                    t.depth + 1 AS depth
                FROM bom_tree t
                JOIN bom_parts b ON t.child_part = b.parent_part
            )
            SELECT 
                child_part,
                total_qty,
                depth
            FROM bom_tree
            ORDER BY depth, child_part;

title: Organizational Reporting Depth & Management Span of Control
human_context: HR analytics measures how deep the management chain is from the CEO to individual contributors and calculates direct vs indirect headcounts for each manager.
hidden_trap: Unbounded recursive queries crash if there is an accidental circular reporting loop (e.g. A reports to B, B reports to A).
duckdb_advantage: DuckDB recursion tracks path depth to prevent infinite loops.
setup_sql:
CREATE TABLE employees (
                emp_id INT,
                emp_name VARCHAR,
                manager_id INT
            );
            INSERT INTO employees VALUES
                (1, 'Alice (CEO)', NULL),
                (2, 'Bob (VP Eng)', 1),
                (3, 'Charlie (VP Sales)', 1),
                (4, 'David (Staff Eng)', 2),
                (5, 'Eve (Senior Eng)', 4);
sql:
-- Traverse management tree from CEO downward, tracking reporting depth
            WITH RECURSIVE org_hierarchy AS (
                SELECT 
                    emp_id,
                    emp_name,
                    manager_id,
                    1 AS hierarchy_level,
                    emp_name AS reporting_path
                FROM employees
                WHERE manager_id IS NULL
                
                UNION ALL
                
                SELECT 
                    e.emp_id,
                    e.emp_name,
                    e.manager_id,
                    h.hierarchy_level + 1,
                    h.reporting_path || ' -> ' || e.emp_name
                FROM employees e
                JOIN org_hierarchy h ON e.manager_id = h.emp_id
            )
            SELECT 
                emp_id,
                emp_name,
                hierarchy_level,
                reporting_path
            FROM org_hierarchy
            ORDER BY hierarchy_level, emp_id;

title: Transitive Fraud Ring & Sybil Account Detection via Device Links
human_context: Financial fraudsters create hundreds of fake accounts linked by shared credit cards, device fingerprints, or IP addresses. Finding all accounts transitively connected to a confirmed fraudster exposes the syndicate.
hidden_trap: Looking only 1 hop away misses fraudsters who funnel funds through mule intermediary accounts.
duckdb_advantage: DuckDB recursive CTEs trace transitive graph edges across multiple hops.
setup_sql:
CREATE TABLE shared_identifiers (
                account_id INT,
                linked_account_id INT
            );
            INSERT INTO shared_identifiers VALUES
                (101, 102), -- 101 shares credit card with 102
                (102, 103), -- 102 shares device with 103
                (103, 104), -- 103 shares bank account with 104
                (201, 202); -- Separate cluster
sql:
-- Find all accounts transitively linked to known bad actor 101
            WITH RECURSIVE fraud_cluster AS (
                SELECT 
                    101 AS seed_account,
                    linked_account_id AS connected_account,
                    1 AS hop_distance
                FROM shared_identifiers
                WHERE account_id = 101
                
                UNION ALL
                
                SELECT 
                    c.seed_account,
                    s.linked_account_id,
                    c.hop_distance + 1
                FROM fraud_cluster c
                JOIN shared_identifiers s ON c.connected_account = s.account_id
                WHERE c.hop_distance < 5
            )
            SELECT DISTINCT 
                seed_account,
                connected_account,
                MIN(hop_distance) AS shortest_hop_distance
            FROM fraud_cluster
            GROUP BY seed_account, connected_account
            ORDER BY shortest_hop_distance;

title: Cycle Detection in Directed Dependency Graphs with Visited Array
human_context: In build systems (e.g. Webpack, Bazel) or task scheduling, circular dependencies (Task A -> Task B -> Task A) cause deadlocks. The engine must detect cycles and abort gracefully.
hidden_trap: Standard recursive CTEs without cycle tracking loop infinitely until the database crashes with out-of-memory errors.
duckdb_advantage: DuckDB array lists (`list_contains`) allow tracking visited paths directly inside recursive CTE state.
setup_sql:
CREATE TABLE task_dependencies (
                task_id VARCHAR,
                depends_on VARCHAR
            );
            INSERT INTO task_dependencies VALUES
                ('compile', 'codegen'),
                ('codegen', 'lint'),
                ('lint', 'compile'); -- Circular cycle!
sql:
-- Detect circular loops using array path tracking
            WITH RECURSIVE path_finder AS (
                SELECT 
                    task_id,
                    depends_on,
                    [task_id] AS visited_path,
                    false AS has_cycle
                FROM task_dependencies
                
                UNION ALL
                
                SELECT 
                    p.task_id,
                    d.depends_on,
                    list_append(p.visited_path, d.task_id),
                    list_contains(p.visited_path, d.depends_on) AS has_cycle
                FROM path_finder p
                JOIN task_dependencies d ON p.depends_on = d.task_id
                WHERE NOT p.has_cycle AND array_length(p.visited_path) < 10
            )
            SELECT 
                task_id,
                depends_on,
                visited_path,
                has_cycle
            FROM path_finder
            WHERE has_cycle = true
            LIMIT 1;

title: Lowest-Cost Routing across Logistics Hubs via Recursive Dijkstra
human_context: Supply chain networks ship containers through intermediary freight hubs. Finding the cheapest transit path from Source to Destination minimizes freight costs.
hidden_trap: Evaluating all combinations without cost bounding leads to exponential path explosion.
duckdb_advantage: DuckDB can evaluate path cost summations in recursive iterations.
sql:
-- Find lowest cost route from Seattle ('SEA') to New York ('JFK')
            WITH RECURSIVE routes AS (
                SELECT 
                    origin,
                    destination,
                    cost AS total_cost,
                    origin || ' -> ' || destination AS route_path,
                    1 AS hops
                FROM shipping_lanes
                WHERE origin = 'SEA'
                
                UNION ALL
                
                SELECT 
                    r.origin,
                    l.destination,
                    r.total_cost + l.cost AS total_cost,
                    r.route_path || ' -> ' || l.destination,
                    r.hops + 1
                FROM routes r
                JOIN shipping_lanes l ON r.destination = l.origin
                WHERE r.hops < 4
            )
            SELECT 
                origin,
                destination,
                total_cost,
                route_path,
                hops
            FROM routes
            WHERE destination = 'JFK'
            ORDER BY total_cost ASC
            LIMIT 1;

title: Causal Microservice Incident Root-Cause Dependency Chain
human_context: When a user checkout fails, it could be caused by payments, auth, database, or network. Tracing dependencies upwards from the affected user service identifies the underlying root-cause service failure.
hidden_trap: Diagnosing downstream symptoms rather than the root upstream failed dependency.
duckdb_advantage: DuckDB traces dependency DAGs and joins failure logs in a single query.
sql:
-- Trace dependencies backwards from checkout-api to find root critical failure
            WITH RECURSIVE upstream_chain AS (
                SELECT 
                    service,
                    depends_on,
                    1 AS depth
                FROM service_mesh
                WHERE service = 'checkout-api'
                
                UNION ALL
                
                SELECT 
                    m.service,
                    m.depends_on,
                    c.depth + 1
                FROM upstream_chain c
                JOIN service_mesh m ON c.depends_on = m.service
            )
            SELECT 
                c.depth,
                c.service,
                c.depends_on AS upstream_service,
                a.status AS upstream_status,
                a.error_rate AS upstream_error_rate
            FROM upstream_chain c
            JOIN service_alerts a ON c.depends_on = a.service
            ORDER BY c.depth DESC
            LIMIT 1;

title: Graph Connected Components Labeling via Min-ID Propagation
human_context: Graph connected components partition isolated clusters of customers or machines. Propagating the minimum account ID across edges assigns every node in the same component a shared group ID.
hidden_trap: Standard SQL engines lack graph primitives, forcing expensive external graph database licenses.
duckdb_advantage: DuckDB can evaluate recursive label propagation directly on relational tables.
sql:
-- Symmetric edges
            WITH RECURSIVE symmetric_edges AS (
                SELECT node_a AS src, node_b AS dst FROM graph_edges
                UNION
                SELECT node_b AS src, node_a AS dst FROM graph_edges
            ),
            components AS (
                -- Anchor: Initial component label is node itself
                SELECT src AS node_id, src AS component_id, 0 AS iteration
                FROM symmetric_edges
                
                UNION ALL
                
                -- Propagate smaller component ID across edges
                SELECT 
                    e.dst AS node_id,
                    c.component_id,
                    c.iteration + 1
                FROM components c
                JOIN symmetric_edges e ON c.node_id = e.src
                WHERE c.component_id < e.dst AND c.iteration < 5
            )
            SELECT 
                node_id,
                MIN(component_id) AS cluster_id
            FROM components
            GROUP BY node_id
            ORDER BY cluster_id, node_id;

title: Network Node In-Degree Centrality and Influence Ranking
human_context: Social network influence and API hub criticality are determined by node in-degree centrality (number of inbound links from distinct entities).
hidden_trap: Counting total edges without filtering distinct source nodes allows a single spammer to inflate influencer metrics.
duckdb_advantage: DuckDB aggregates high-volume graph degree metrics with high-speed hash grouping.
setup_sql:
CREATE TABLE network_follows (
                follower_id INT,
                target_user_id INT
            );
            INSERT INTO network_follows VALUES
                (101, 1), (102, 1), (103, 1), (104, 1), -- Node 1 has 4 followers
                (101, 2), (102, 2),                     -- Node 2 has 2 followers
                (101, 3);                               -- Node 3 has 1 follower
sql:
-- Compute in-degree centrality and influence rank
            SELECT 
                target_user_id AS influencer_id,
                COUNT(DISTINCT follower_id) AS in_degree_centrality,
                DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY COUNT(DISTINCT follower_id) DESC) AS influence_rank
            FROM network_follows
            GROUP BY target_user_id
            ORDER BY influence_rank;

title: Task Scheduling Critical Path Method (CPM) Duration Analysis
human_context: Project managers identify the 'Critical Path'—the longest sequence of dependent tasks that dictates the minimum project completion time.
hidden_trap: Adding task durations without considering parallel execution branches yields an unrealistically inflated project timeline.
duckdb_advantage: DuckDB recursive CTEs trace parallel branch durations and calculate maximum path length.
setup_sql:
CREATE TABLE project_tasks (
                task_code VARCHAR,
                prerequisite_code VARCHAR,
                duration_days INT
            );
            INSERT INTO project_tasks VALUES
                ('START', NULL, 0),
                ('DESIGN', 'START', 10),
                ('BUILD_FRONTEND', 'DESIGN', 15),
                ('BUILD_BACKEND',  'DESIGN', 25), -- Longest branch
                ('DEPLOY', 'BUILD_BACKEND', 5);
sql:
-- Find the longest path (Critical Path) from START to DEPLOY
            WITH RECURSIVE task_paths AS (
                SELECT 
                    task_code,
                    duration_days AS cumulative_days,
                    task_code AS path_str
                FROM project_tasks
                WHERE prerequisite_code IS NULL
                
                UNION ALL
                
                SELECT 
                    t.task_code,
                    p.cumulative_days + t.duration_days,
                    p.path_str || ' -> ' || t.task_code
                FROM task_paths p
                JOIN project_tasks t ON p.task_code = t.prerequisite_code
            )
            SELECT 
                task_code,
                cumulative_days AS critical_path_duration,
                path_str
            FROM task_paths
            ORDER BY cumulative_days DESC
            LIMIT 1;

title: Multi-Level Affiliate Referral Tree Commission Rollup (Tier 1-3)
human_context: Affiliate programs reward referrals up to 3 tiers deep (Direct referrer gets 10%, Tier 2 gets 5%, Tier 3 gets 2.5% of purchase amount).
hidden_trap: Hardcoded 3-way self-joins fail to handle users whose upline is only 1 or 2 tiers deep without complex coalesce logic.
duckdb_advantage: DuckDB recursive CTEs assign dynamic commission percentages based on recursion depth.
setup_sql:
CREATE TABLE referral_links (
                user_id INT,
                referrer_id INT
            );
            CREATE TABLE user_purchases (
                purchase_id INT,
                user_id INT,
                amount DECIMAL(10,2)
            );
            INSERT INTO referral_links VALUES
                (4, 3), -- 4 referred by 3
                (3, 2), -- 3 referred by 2
                (2, 1); -- 2 referred by 1 (Grandparent)
            INSERT INTO user_purchases VALUES
                (101, 4, 1000.00); -- Purchase by user 4
sql:
-- Calculate multi-tier referral payout for purchase 101
            WITH RECURSIVE upline AS (
                -- Level 1: Direct referrer
                SELECT 
                    r.user_id AS buyer_id,
                    r.referrer_id AS beneficiary_id,
                    1 AS tier,
                    0.10 AS commission_rate
                FROM referral_links r
                WHERE r.user_id = 4
                
                UNION ALL
                
                -- Level 2 and 3 upline
                SELECT 
                    u.buyer_id,
                    r.referrer_id AS beneficiary_id,
                    u.tier + 1,
                    CASE WHEN u.tier + 1 = 2 THEN 0.05 ELSE 0.025 END AS commission_rate
                FROM upline u
                JOIN referral_links r ON u.beneficiary_id = r.user_id
                WHERE u.tier < 3
            )
            SELECT 
                u.buyer_id,
                u.beneficiary_id,
                u.tier,
                p.amount AS purchase_amount,
                ROUND(p.amount * u.commission_rate, 2) AS commission_earned
            FROM upline u
            JOIN user_purchases p ON u.buyer_id = p.user_id
            ORDER BY u.tier;

title: Multi-Parent Shared Infrastructure Cost Allocation Rollup
human_context: Cloud infrastructure (e.g. shared Kubernetes cluster) is co-owned by multiple products with fractional split percentages. Costs must cascade down to consumer business units.
hidden_trap: Failing to multiply split percentages down the DAG results in allocated costs exceeding 100% of actual spend.
duckdb_advantage: DuckDB calculates fractional cost propagation with exact decimal precision.
sql:
-- Allocate parent cost to child business units
            SELECT 
                a.parent_node,
                a.child_node,
                a.allocation_pct,
                n.monthly_cost AS raw_parent_cost,
                ROUND(n.monthly_cost * a.allocation_pct, 2) AS allocated_cost
            FROM cost_allocations a
            JOIN cost_nodes n ON a.parent_node = n.node_id
            ORDER BY allocated_cost DESC;

title: Triangular FX Currency Arbitrage Detection (Loop Profitability)
human_context: High-frequency FX trading bots scan for triangular arbitrage where converting USD -> EUR -> JPY -> USD yields more than 1.00 USD after exchange rates.
hidden_trap: Missing currency conversion bid-ask spreads causes false positive arbitrage signals that lose money in practice.
duckdb_advantage: DuckDB evaluates 3-hop currency cycles and product rates in sub-millisecond execution.
setup_sql:
CREATE TABLE fx_pairs (
                from_curr VARCHAR,
                to_curr VARCHAR,
                exchange_rate DOUBLE
            );
            INSERT INTO fx_pairs VALUES
                ('USD', 'EUR', 0.92),
                ('EUR', 'JPY', 160.0),
                ('JPY', 'USD', 0.0069); -- Arbitrage loop: 0.92 * 160 * 0.0069 = 1.01568 (+1.5% profit)
sql:
-- Detect 3-hop triangular arbitrage opportunities where effective rate > 1.005
            SELECT 
                a.from_curr AS curr_start,
                a.to_curr AS curr_mid1,
                b.to_curr AS curr_mid2,
                c.to_curr AS curr_end,
                ROUND(a.exchange_rate * b.exchange_rate * c.exchange_rate, 4) AS loop_multiplier,
                ROUND((a.exchange_rate * b.exchange_rate * c.exchange_rate - 1.0) * 100, 2) AS profit_margin_pct
            FROM fx_pairs a
            JOIN fx_pairs b ON a.to_curr = b.from_curr
            JOIN fx_pairs c ON b.to_curr = c.from_curr AND c.to_curr = a.from_curr
            WHERE (a.exchange_rate * b.exchange_rate * c.exchange_rate) > 1.005;

title: Transactional State Machine Transition Sequence Verification
human_context: Financial compliance requires payment transactions to strictly follow the state sequence: INITIATED -> AUTHORIZED -> CAPTURED -> SETTLED. Any transaction skipping steps is flagged as fraudulent.
hidden_trap: Verifying status counts without checking transition sequence allows out-of-order state transitions.
duckdb_advantage: DuckDB LEAD/LAG checks verify exact valid transition edges against a legal state graph.
sql:
-- Validate that every state transition matches the legal state machine rules
            WITH transitions AS (
                SELECT 
                    tx_id,
                    status AS current_state,
                    LEAD(status) OVER (PARTITION BY tx_id ORDER BY step_order) AS next_state
                FROM payment_status_audit
            )
            SELECT 
                tx_id,
                current_state,
                next_state,
                CASE 
                    WHEN next_state IS NULL THEN 'TERMINAL_STATE'
                    WHEN current_state = 'INITIATED' AND next_state = 'AUTHORIZED' THEN 'VALID'
                    WHEN current_state = 'AUTHORIZED' AND next_state = 'CAPTURED' THEN 'VALID'
                    WHEN current_state = 'CAPTURED' AND next_state = 'SETTLED' THEN 'VALID'
                    ELSE 'INVALID_ILLEGAL_STATE_JUMP'
                END AS audit_validation_result
            FROM transitions
            ORDER BY tx_id, current_state;

title: Chasm Trap Resolution: Multi-Table 1:N Aggregation without Fan-Out Inflation
human_context: When an order has multiple discounts AND multiple shipment records, joining both child tables directly to the order creates a cross product that multiplies sales figures by 4x. Pre-aggregating each child table in CTEs before joining preserves financial integrity.
hidden_trap: Frontier models routinely join all tables before GROUP BY, causing catastrophic silent metric corruption.
duckdb_advantage: DuckDB can evaluate pre-aggregated CTEs in parallel vector pipelines with zero temp-table writes.
sql:
-- Correctly aggregate discounts and shipments without fan-out inflation
            WITH agg_discounts AS (
                SELECT order_id, SUM(amount) AS total_discount
                FROM order_discounts
                GROUP BY order_id
            ),
            agg_shipments AS (
                SELECT order_id, SUM(fee) AS total_shipping
                FROM order_shipments
                GROUP BY order_id
            )
            SELECT 
                o.customer_id,
                SUM(o.base_amount) AS total_gross_sales,
                COALESCE(SUM(d.total_discount), 0.00) AS total_discount_amount,
                COALESCE(SUM(s.total_shipping), 0.00) AS total_shipping_fees,
                ROUND(SUM(o.base_amount) - COALESCE(SUM(d.total_discount), 0.00) + COALESCE(SUM(s.total_shipping), 0.00), 2) AS net_revenue
            FROM orders o
            LEFT JOIN agg_discounts d ON o.order_id = d.order_id
            LEFT JOIN agg_shipments s ON o.order_id = s.order_id
            GROUP BY o.customer_id;

title: Three-Valued Logic Safe Anti-Join (Eliminating the NOT IN NULL Trap)
human_context: Marketing queries to find active customers who have not churned often use `WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT customer_id FROM churned_users)`. If a single `NULL` exists in `churned_users`, SQL three-valued logic causes the entire query to return ZERO rows.
hidden_trap: In SQL, `val NOT IN (1, NULL)` evaluates to `UNKNOWN`, which evaluates to `FALSE` in WHERE clauses, silently discarding every single record.
duckdb_advantage: Using `NOT EXISTS` or `ANTI JOIN` avoids three-valued logic traps and compiles to optimal hash anti-joins.
sql:
-- Robust anti-join that is immune to NULL records in the subquery
            SELECT 
                c.customer_id,
                c.name
            FROM all_customers c
            WHERE NOT EXISTS (
                SELECT 1 
                FROM churned_customers ch 
                WHERE ch.customer_id = c.customer_id
            )
            ORDER BY c.customer_id;

title: List Lambdas for High-Performance Nested Array Transformations
human_context: Modern analytical warehouses store nested array payloads (e.g. array of discount percentages). Transforming or filtering elements directly inside the array without unnesting and re-aggregating saves massive compute.
hidden_trap: Unnesting arrays to flat rows and re-aggregating with LIST() triggers expensive hash shuffles.
duckdb_advantage: DuckDB list lambdas (`list_transform`, `list_filter`) execute in-place vectorized functions directly on array vectors.
sql:
-- Filter out discounts <= 5% and double remaining discount percentages using list lambdas
            SELECT 
                cart_id,
                discounts_applied AS raw_discounts,
                list_filter(discounts_applied, lambda x: x > 5) AS qualifying_discounts,
                list_transform(
                    list_filter(discounts_applied, lambda x: x > 5), 
                    lambda x: x * 2
                ) AS doubled_qualifying_discounts
            FROM shopping_carts
            ORDER BY cart_id;

title: Median Absolute Deviation (MAD) Robust Statistical Outlier Detection
human_context: Traditional standard deviation Z-scores fail in the presence of extreme outliers because the outliers themselves distort the mean and standard deviation. MAD is a robust statistical scale estimator.
hidden_trap: Mean and standard deviation break down completely on fat-tailed or skewed data distributions.
duckdb_advantage: DuckDB can compute medians of deviations in standard analytical CTEs.
setup_sql:
CREATE TABLE payment_volumes (
                tx_id INT,
                amount DOUBLE
            );
            INSERT INTO payment_volumes VALUES
                (1, 10.0), (2, 12.0), (3, 11.0), (4, 13.0), (5, 12.0),
                (6, 1000.0); -- Massive outlier
sql:
-- Compute Median Absolute Deviation (MAD) and flag robust outliers
            -- MAD = MEDIAN( |x - MEDIAN(x)| )
            WITH med AS (
                SELECT MEDIAN(amount) AS overall_median
                FROM payment_volumes
            ),
            deviations AS (
                SELECT 
                    p.tx_id,
                    p.amount,
                    m.overall_median,
                    ABS(p.amount - m.overall_median) AS abs_deviation
                FROM payment_volumes p
                CROSS JOIN med m
            ),
            mad_val AS (
                SELECT MEDIAN(abs_deviation) AS mad_score
                FROM deviations
            )
            SELECT 
                d.tx_id,
                d.amount,
                d.overall_median,
                ROUND(d.abs_deviation / NULLIF(v.mad_score, 0), 2) AS robust_mad_score,
                CASE 
                    WHEN (d.abs_deviation / NULLIF(v.mad_score, 0)) > 3.0 
                    THEN 'ROBUST_OUTLIER' 
                    ELSE 'NORMAL' 
                END AS anomaly_flag
            FROM deviations d
            CROSS JOIN mad_val v
            ORDER BY robust_mad_score DESC;

title: Robust Z-Score Normalization using Median and Interquartile Range (IQR)
human_context: Standardizing skewed metrics (like API response latency) for machine learning feature pipelines requires scaling by IQR (Q3 - Q1) rather than standard deviation.
hidden_trap: Standard Z-score produces biased features when distributions have heavy tails.
duckdb_advantage: DuckDB percentile functions (`QUANTILE_CONT`) compute exact quartiles in a single scan.
sql:
-- Compute robust IQR-normalized score: (x - Q2) / (Q3 - Q1)
            WITH quartiles AS (
                SELECT 
                    QUANTILE_CONT(latency_ms, 0.25) AS q1,
                    QUANTILE_CONT(latency_ms, 0.50) AS median_val,
                    QUANTILE_CONT(latency_ms, 0.75) AS q3
                FROM response_times
            )
            SELECT 
                r.request_id,
                r.latency_ms,
                ROUND((r.latency_ms - q.median_val) / NULLIF(q.q3 - q.q1, 0), 3) AS robust_iqr_z_score
            FROM response_times r
            CROSS JOIN quartiles q
            ORDER BY robust_iqr_z_score DESC;

title: Financial Ledger Running Total: ROWS vs. RANGE Semantic Contrast
human_context: In financial auditing, understanding the exact behavioral difference between `ROWS BETWEEN` and `RANGE BETWEEN` prevents duplicate-timestamp errors from failing regulatory ledger reconciliations.
hidden_trap: The ANSI SQL default for window frames with ORDER BY is `RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW`, which aggregates identical peers together into one lump sum.
duckdb_advantage: DuckDB provides explicit window execution options and deterministic ordering.
sql:
-- Compare the difference between default RANGE (peer bunching) vs ROWS (strict sequential)
            SELECT 
                tx_id,
                val_date,
                amount,
                -- Default RANGE behavior: bunches tied dates together ($150 on row 1 and 2)
                SUM(amount) OVER (
                    ORDER BY val_date
                    RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
                ) AS bunched_range_total,
                -- Explicit ROWS behavior: increments strictly row by row ($100 then $150)
                SUM(amount) OVER (
                    ORDER BY val_date, tx_id
                    ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
                ) AS strict_rows_total
            FROM audit_ledger
            ORDER BY val_date, tx_id;

title: SARGable Partition Pruning: Exact Half-Open Date Boundary Ranges
human_context: When filtering analytical partitions for a calendar month, `BETWEEN '2026-01-01' AND '2026-01-31'` leaks into February 1st if timestamps contain hours/minutes, while `strftime('%m', ts) = '01'` disables partition pruning entirely.
hidden_trap: Subtle boundary leakage or full table scans caused by non-SARGable WHERE predicates.
duckdb_advantage: Half-open `>= '2026-01-01' AND < '2026-02-01'` ensures exact month boundaries and 100% metadata partition pruning.
sql:
-- Exact SARGable half-open January 2026 boundary query
            SELECT 
                event_id,
                created_at
            FROM audit_events
            WHERE created_at >= TIMESTAMP '2026-01-01 00:00:00'
              AND created_at <  TIMESTAMP '2026-02-01 00:00:00'
            ORDER BY created_at;

title: Window Peer Frame Exclusion: EXCLUDE GROUP for Clean Cross-Group Contrast
human_context: When comparing sales across product categories or dates, analysts want to compute the average of all other groups, strictly excluding the entire current group.
hidden_trap: Computing group baselines without excluding the current group dilutes contrast in small sample sizes.
duckdb_advantage: DuckDB fully supports SQL:2011 `EXCLUDE GROUP` window syntax.
sql:
-- Compute baseline average across other regions strictly excluding current region group
            SELECT 
                region,
                order_id,
                sale_amount,
                ROUND(AVG(sale_amount) OVER (
                    ORDER BY region
                    ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING
                    EXCLUDE GROUP
                ), 2) AS other_regions_baseline_avg
            FROM regional_orders
            ORDER BY region, order_id;

title: Window Frame Ties Exclusion: EXCLUDE TIES for Unbiased Cumulative Totals
human_context: In financial ranking, when multiple entities have the exact same score, evaluating cumulative rank metrics without self-reinforcing duplicate ties prevents tied participants from skewing percentiles.
hidden_trap: Tied participants mutually inflate each other's cumulative metrics.
duckdb_advantage: DuckDB supports `EXCLUDE TIES` in window frames.
sql:
-- Calculate cumulative score excluding tied peers at the current rank
            SELECT 
                player_id,
                score,
                SUM(score) OVER (
                    ORDER BY score DESC
                    RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
                    EXCLUDE TIES
                ) AS cumulative_score_excluding_tied_peers
            FROM gaming_scores
            ORDER BY score DESC, player_id;

title: Market Basket Association Rules: Support, Confidence, and Lift in Pure SQL
human_context: Data miners discover product affinities ('Customers who buy Item A also buy Item B') using Support, Confidence, and Lift metrics computed directly from transaction tables.
hidden_trap: Generating cross-products across all transactions creates memory spills on large catalogs.
duckdb_advantage: DuckDB can evaluate pair frequency matrices and marginal probabilities in memory.
sql:
-- Compute Support, Confidence, and Lift for Item A -> Item B
            WITH basket_totals AS (
                SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT order_id) AS total_baskets FROM order_baskets
            ),
            item_counts AS (
                SELECT item, COUNT(DISTINCT order_id) AS item_baskets
                FROM order_baskets
                GROUP BY item
            ),
            pair_counts AS (
                SELECT 
                    a.item AS item_a,
                    b.item AS item_b,
                    COUNT(DISTINCT a.order_id) AS pair_baskets
                FROM order_baskets a
                JOIN order_baskets b 
                  ON a.order_id = b.order_id 
                 AND a.item != b.item
                GROUP BY a.item, b.item
            )
            SELECT 
                p.item_a,
                p.item_b,
                p.pair_baskets,
                -- Support: P(A and B)
                ROUND(p.pair_baskets * 1.0 / t.total_baskets, 3) AS support,
                -- Confidence: P(B | A) = pair / count_a
                ROUND(p.pair_baskets * 1.0 / ca.item_baskets, 3) AS confidence,
                -- Lift: Confidence / P(B) = (pair * total) / (count_a * count_b)
                ROUND((p.pair_baskets * 1.0 * t.total_baskets) / (ca.item_baskets * cb.item_baskets), 3) AS lift
            FROM pair_counts p
            JOIN item_counts ca ON p.item_a = ca.item
            JOIN item_counts cb ON p.item_b = cb.item
            CROSS JOIN basket_totals t
            WHERE p.pair_baskets >= 2
            ORDER BY lift DESC, p.item_a, p.item_b;

title: Kaplan-Meier Non-Parametric Customer Survival Analysis in SQL
human_context: Actuarial and SaaS subscription models estimate the probability of customer survival past Day T, accounting for right-censored users who haven't churned yet.
hidden_trap: Naively dividing churned users by total signups underestimates customer lifetime value.
duckdb_advantage: DuckDB window functions compute step-down survival curves using cumulative products.
setup_sql:
CREATE TABLE subscription_cohort (
                user_id INT,
                tenure_months INT,
                has_churned BOOLEAN
            );
            INSERT INTO subscription_cohort VALUES
                (1, 1, true),  -- Churned at month 1
                (2, 1, false), -- Still active at month 1
                (3, 2, true),  -- Churned at month 2
                (4, 2, false),
                (5, 3, false);
sql:
-- Kaplan-Meier survival probability estimation by tenure month
            WITH monthly_risk AS (
                SELECT 
                    tenure_months,
                    COUNT(*) AS cohort_events,
                    SUM(CASE WHEN has_churned THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS churn_count,
                    COUNT(*) OVER (ORDER BY tenure_months DESC ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS number_at_risk
                FROM subscription_cohort
                GROUP BY tenure_months
            )
            SELECT 
                tenure_months,
                number_at_risk,
                churn_count,
                ROUND(1.0 - (churn_count * 1.0 / number_at_risk), 4) AS interval_survival_rate
            FROM monthly_risk
            ORDER BY tenure_months;

title: Dynamic Equi-Depth Histogram Binning via NTILE in Pure SQL
human_context: Creating balanced feature histograms for ML requires equal-depth binning (each bucket contains an equal number of records) rather than equal-width binning.
hidden_trap: Equal-width bins leave high-value tail bins completely empty on skewed power-law distributions.
duckdb_advantage: DuckDB `NTILE()` computes equi-depth quantile bins with zero pre-scanning.
sql:
-- Partition customers into 4 equal-depth spending quartiles (bins)
            WITH binned AS (
                SELECT 
                    customer_id,
                    annual_spend,
                    NTILE(4) OVER (ORDER BY annual_spend ASC) AS spend_quartile
                FROM customer_spend
            )
            SELECT 
                spend_quartile,
                COUNT(*) AS customer_count,
                MIN(annual_spend) AS min_spend_in_bin,
                MAX(annual_spend) AS max_spend_in_bin,
                ROUND(AVG(annual_spend), 2) AS avg_spend_in_bin
            FROM binned
            GROUP BY spend_quartile
            ORDER BY spend_quartile;
